## Audit: `docs/w8-close-out` vs `main`

Scope: `CLAUDE.md` (§13) and `docs/progress.md`, per `git diff main...HEAD`.

### Findings

**1. Week 8 section internal consistency — clean**
- `docs/progress.md:394-430` (the Week-8 section body): every row is `[x] ✅`, no remaining `⬜`/`🟡` markers.
- Aggregate table (`docs/progress.md:446-454`): Week 8 row `29 | 0 | 0 | 29`; column sums `10+17+18+26+18+28+41+29 = 187` (matches `TOTAL` Done), pending sum `0+2+0+0+0+0+0+0 = 2` (matches `TOTAL` Pending), total-column sum `= 189` (matches `TOTAL` Total). `TOTAL 187/0/2/189` is internally consistent.
- No issues here.

**2. Coverage/test numbers — consistent, no stale leftovers**
- `98.3` / `1273` / `87.8` / `334` all appear the same number of times, consistently, in both `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/progress.md`. No `1233`/`349`/`86.6`/`~91%`/`~80%` stragglers found anywhere. The one place an old number is retained (`91% backend, ~80% frontend`) was removed — confirmed absent.
- `docs/progress.md:417` correctly updates "47 test files" → "53 test files total" for the frontend section.
- `docs/progress.md:432` labels the coverage numbers "at close" and `CLAUDE.md:286`/`docs/progress.md:18` label them "at flip" — correctly scoped, not presented as stale.

**3. Issue register — 🔴 does not match GitHub reality**
Both files claim **52 open issues = 2 Week-8 (`#177`, `#553`) + 50 backlog**, and both explicitly assert **`#128` is closed** "with this close-out":

**6. Superseded-parenthetical wraps — 🔴 malformed italics (odd underscore count)**
Both new wraps contain exactly **3** underscores each (an odd count), which does not close correctly in Markdown:

- `CLAUDE.md:303` — `_(Prior-week detail:_ ... #461).)_`
- `docs/progress.md:28` — `_(Superseded W8-cycle detail:_ ... #550.)_`

Pattern: `_(Label:_ <huge block> )_`. The first `_` opens italics, the second `_` (right after `Label:`) immediately closes it — so **only the label itself renders italicized**, e.g. *"(Prior-week detail:"* — and the entire following block (the actual superseded/prior-week content) renders as **plain, non-italic text**. The final `_` at the very end has no partner left to pair with in that paragraph/table-cell and will render as a **literal stray underscore character** right after the closing `)`.

Net effect on render: `*(Prior-week detail:*` Week 7 closed ... `#461).)_` — with a visible trailing `_` glyph and no italics over the superseded block, which is presumably not the intended visual (the intent looks like "italicize the whole deferred block, with a bold-ish label").

**Suggested fix:** drop the underscore immediately after the label colon so there's exactly one open/close pair spanning the whole parenthetical, e.g.:
`_(Prior-week detail: Week 7 closed ... #461).)_`
(single `_` at the very start, single `_` at the very end, nothing in between) — this italicizes the entire block as apparently intended. Apply the same fix to the `docs/progress.md:28` "Superseded W8-cycle detail" wrap.

        # Synchronous CVE gate over the entire runtime + test dependency tree

        # PyPI/OSV advisory DB. Complements the Dependabot alerts (full graph,
        # async) with a fail-fast merge check.
        #
        # The 5 ignored advisories are cryptography + pyOpenSSL CVEs blocked by
        # snowflake-connector-python<4 / snowflake-sqlalchemy<4 — a deliberate
        # major datasource bump tracked in #129 (the deadline for removing these).
        #
        # Bounded retry: pip-audit resolves the requirements file via PyPI's
        # per-package JSON endpoint, so a single transient PyPI/OSV 5xx (e.g.
        # "503 Backend is unhealthy") aborts the whole audit and flakes the gate.
        # Retrying with backoff absorbs that *without* masking real findings — a
        # genuine CVE fails every attempt and still blocks (90s worst-case backoff).
        run: |
          audit() {
            pip-audit -r backend/requirements-dev.txt \
              --ignore-vuln PYSEC-2026-36 \
              --ignore-vuln PYSEC-2026-35 \
              --ignore-vuln CVE-2026-26007 \
              --ignore-vuln CVE-2026-27448 \
              --ignore-vuln CVE-2026-27459
          }
          for attempt in 1 2 3 4; do
            if audit; then
              exit 0
            fi
            if [ "$attempt" -lt 4 ]; then
              echo "::warning::pip-audit attempt $attempt failed (likely a transient PyPI/OSV 5xx) — retrying in $((attempt * 15))s"
              sleep $((attempt * 15))
            fi
          done
          echo "::error::pip-audit failed after 4 attempts — a real CVE or a persistent PyPI/OSV outage (see log above)"
          exit 1

# Frontend mutation testing (Stryker)

The frontend analogue of the backend mutmut spike ([CONTRIBUTING rule 4a](../../CONTRIBUTING.md)).
**Manual / periodic, never CI** — mutation testing is too slow to gate merges, and
its big tool tree shouldn't sit on the `pnpm audit` surface. So, like the backend's
standalone `requirements-mutation.txt`, **Stryker is not a dependency in
`frontend/package.json`** — [`run.sh`](./run.sh) installs it ad-hoc (pinned) and
restores the manifest on exit.

## Run a spike

```bash
frontend/mutation/run.sh                                  # mutate the configured target
frontend/mutation/run.sh --mutate 'src/components/checks/checkForm.ts'
```

Config lives in [`../stryker.conf.json`](../stryker.conf.json); the version pin is in
`run.sh`. The default `mutate` target is `suiteTarget.ts` — point it at whatever pure
module you're hardening (the conversion/resolver utils are the best targets:
`suiteTarget.ts`, `checkForm.ts`, `expectationCatalog.ts`, `resultsFormat.ts`).

## Reading the result

Stryker prints a `[Survived]` block per mutant the tests failed to kill, plus a
mutation-score table. Triage each survivor:

- **Real gap** — a behavioural mutation (flipped condition, dropped branch, changed
  return) that no test caught. Add/strengthen a test. This is the point of the spike.
- **Equivalent mutant** — a change with no observable effect (e.g. mutating a value
  that's re-narrowed downstream, or an unreachable branch). Not a gap; leave it.
/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/requirements-mutation.txt:4:# mutmut and its transitive deps (libcst, parso, textual, …) stay OFF the CI
/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/requirements-mutation.txt:10:# 3.x is a ground-up rewrite (config in pyproject `[tool.mutmut]`, copies the tree
/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/requirements-mutation.txt:12:# `mutmut results`/`show` on Python 3.13 (#253), so reporting works natively again.
/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/requirements-mutation.txt:16:mutmut==3.6.0

import fs from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';

import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';

// One interactive login per session: launches a HEADED browser at the live
// URL, waits for a human to complete the real OIDC sign-in (MFA and all), then
// serializes sessionStorage to a gitignored file the specs replay via
// addInitScript. sessionStorage (not cookies/localStorage) because
// oidc-client-ts keeps the signed-in user there (authClient.ts
// WebStorageStateStore) — Playwright's built-in storageState can't capture it.
//
// The captured token expires like any AAD token (~1h); the file is reused
// while fresh and re-captured otherwise.

// cwd-relative (pnpm runs from frontend/): __dirname doesn't exist under ESM.
export const SESSION_FILE = path.resolve('e2e-live', '.auth', 'session.json');
const MAX_AGE_MS = 40 * 60 * 1000; // re-login when the capture is older than 40 min

export default async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  const liveBaseURL = process.env.E2E_LIVE_BASE_URL;
  if (!liveBaseURL) {
    throw new Error('live-smoke lane requires E2E_LIVE_BASE_URL');
  }
  // Stat-and-use (no exists pre-check — CodeQL js/file-system-race): a missing
  // file just means "no capture yet".
  let capturedAtMs = 0;
  try {
    capturedAtMs = fs.statSync(SESSION_FILE).mtimeMs;
  } catch {
    // no session captured yet
  }
  if (capturedAtMs && Date.now() - capturedAtMs < MAX_AGE_MS) {
    return; // fresh enough — reuse
  }

  const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto(liveBaseURL);
  console.log('\n[live-smoke] Complete the sign-in in the opened browser…');
  // The post-login landing is the Dashboard; give MFA up to 5 minutes.
  await page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard', level: 3 }).waitFor({ timeout: 300_000 });
  const session: string = await page.evaluate(() => JSON.stringify({ ...sessionStorage }));
  fs.mkdirSync(path.dirname(SESSION_FILE), { recursive: true });
  // Temp-write + rename: atomic replace, and no write decision hangs off the
  // earlier stat (a parallel capture just loses the rename race harmlessly).
  const tmp = `${SESSION_FILE}.${process.pid}.tmp`;
  fs.writeFileSync(tmp, session);
  fs.renameSync(tmp, SESSION_FILE);
  await browser.close();
  console.log('[live-smoke] Session captured.');
}

1	# Azure AD SSO app registrations (real auth in prod; AUTH_DEV_BYPASS=false). The
2	# backend's init_auth() requires AZURE_API_CLIENT_ID + AZURE_TENANT_ID at startup
3	# and validates v2 access tokens; the SPA (generic OIDC client, ADR 0028) uses
4	# AZURE_SPA_CLIENT_ID with a redirect URI of the frontend origin. Two registrations:
5	#   - API  (dataq-app-api-sso): exposes the `user_impersonation` scope, v2 tokens.
6	#   - SPA  (dataq-app-spa): public single-page client, redirect = frontend origin,
7	#                           pre-authorized on the API scope (no consent prompt).
8	
9	data "azuread_client_config" "current" {}
10	
11	resource "random_uuid" "api_scope" {}
12	
13	# ── API app registration ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
14	resource "azuread_application" "api" {
15	  display_name = "dataq-app-api-sso"
16	  owners       = [data.azuread_client_config.current.object_id]
17	
18	  api {
19	    requested_access_token_version = 2 # v2 tokens (login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0)
20	
21	    oauth2_permission_scope {
22	      id                         = random_uuid.api_scope.result
23	      value                      = var.azure_api_scope
24	      type                       = "User"
25	      enabled                    = true
26	      admin_consent_display_name = "Access the DataQ API"
27	      admin_consent_description  = "Allow the application to access the DataQ API on behalf of the signed-in user."
28	      user_consent_display_name  = "Access the DataQ API"
29	      user_consent_description   = "Allow the application to access the DataQ API on your behalf."
30	    }
31	  }
32	
33	  # The Application ID URI (api://<client_id>) is managed by the separate
34	  # azuread_application_identifier_uri.api resource below. Without this, the
35	  # provider treats the URI as drift on THIS resource and removes it on every
36	  # apply — which strips the API's token audience and breaks SSO. Ignore it here;
37	  # the dedicated resource stays the source of truth.
38	  lifecycle {
39	    ignore_changes = [identifier_uris]
40	  }
41	}
42	
43	# api://<client_id> identifier URI (separate resource — needs the client_id known).
44	resource "azuread_application_identifier_uri" "api" {
45	  application_id = azuread_application.api.id
46	  identifier_uri = "api://${azuread_application.api.client_id}"
47	}
48	
49	resource "azuread_service_principal" "api" {
50	  client_id = azuread_application.api.client_id
51	  owners    = [data.azuread_client_config.current.object_id]
52	}
53	
54	# ── SPA app registration ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
55	resource "azuread_application" "spa" {
56	  display_name = "dataq-app-spa"
57	  owners       = [data.azuread_client_config.current.object_id]
58	
59	  single_page_application {
60	    # Azure AD requires a trailing slash when there's no path segment; the OIDC
61	    # client's redirect_uri is `${window.location.origin}/` to match exactly
62	    # (frontend/src/auth/authClient.ts, generic OIDC per ADR 0028). The origin is
63	    # the frontend Container App (ADR 0028 §5 cutover), computed from the env
64	    # domain (local.frontend_url) to avoid a resource-reference cycle.
65	    redirect_uris = ["${local.frontend_url}/"]
66	  }
67	
68	  # Request the API's user_impersonation scope.
69	  required_resource_access {
70	    resource_app_id = azuread_application.api.client_id
71	    resource_access {
72	      id   = random_uuid.api_scope.result
73	      type = "Scope"
74	    }
75	  }
76	
77	  # Microsoft Graph User.Read (sign-in + read profile).
78	  required_resource_access {
79	    resource_app_id = "00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000"
80	    resource_access {
81	      id   = "e1fe6dd8-ba31-4d61-89e7-88639da4683d" # User.Read
82	      type = "Scope"
83	    }
84	  }
85	}
86	
87	resource "azuread_service_principal" "spa" {
88	  client_id = azuread_application.spa.client_id
89	  owners    = [data.azuread_client_config.current.object_id]
90	}
91	
92	# Pre-authorize the SPA on the API scope so users aren't prompted to consent to
93	# the custom API (same-tenant, single product).
94	resource "azuread_application_pre_authorized" "spa_on_api" {
95	  application_id       = azuread_application.api.id
96	  authorized_client_id = azuread_application.spa.client_id
97	  permission_ids       = [random_uuid.api_scope.result]
98	}
99	
```

## Operational notes

- **Restart dependent Container Apps after a shared-Postgres delete/recreate** —
  the DB host is injected as a start-time secret snapshot, so every dependent
  revision must be restarted or it keeps resolving the old/dead host.
- The shared RG / Container Apps env / Postgres server are **reused, never
  destroyed** (free/trial caps one of each; shared with the harness — ADR 0024).
- `key_vault_purge_protection` is off during bring-up (so a destroy/re-apply can
  reuse the vault name); set it **true** for a hardened prod (irreversible).
  **Decision (2026-07-02): deliberately left off** for this deployment — the vault
  is demo/trial-scoped and destroy/re-apply flexibility wins; every secret it holds
  (PATs, SAS, webhook secrets) is rotatable, so accidental-delete recovery is
  re-mint, not data loss. Revisit (flip to `true`) before any regulated or
  production-critical use.
- **Workspace-admins are superusers over every suite** ([ADR 0027](../docs/adr/0027-suite-permission-model-workspace-admin.md) / #482):
  anyone in `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` can read **all** suites' results — including
  failing-row samples (`results.sample_failures`), the one place PII/PHI lands —
  and manage/delete any suite. **Keep the allowlist minimal.** For a **PHI / regulated
  deployment**, treat the data-access audit trail (G1 / #431 in
  [compliance-posture.md](../docs/compliance-posture.md)) as a **prerequisite before
  granting broad workspace-admin** — PHI is already G1-blocked, and this access breadth
  raises the bar.
```

@@ -270,6 +270,16 @@ proxy; `<frontend>/api/v1/...` is the base URL for any external client too):
   (PATs, SAS, webhook secrets) is rotatable, so accidental-delete recovery is

   production-critical use.
+- **Azure CLI is pre-authorized on the API scope** (`azuread_application_pre_authorized.azure_cli_on_api`
+  in `terraform/azure/sso.tf`): operators mint API bearers non-interactively with
+  `az account get-access-token --resource api://<api-client-id>` (live smoke,
+  `e2e_smoke.py` `DATAQ_BEARER` mode, MCP clients). The signed-in Azure user must
+  still exist in DataQ's user model to see anything (suite-scoped authz applies as
+  normal — a token for an unknown/unshared user reads an empty workspace). The
+  grant was first applied manually via Graph on 2026-07-03; if your state predates
+  it, `terraform import` the existing grant instead of recreating:
+  `terraform import azuread_application_pre_authorized.azure_cli_on_api <api-application-object-id>/preAuthorizedApplication/04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46`.
+  Interim posture until ADR 0026 (DataQ-issued API keys) is decided.
 - **Workspace-admins are superusers over every suite** ([ADR 0027](../docs/adr/0027-suite-permission-model-workspace-admin.md) / #482):
   anyone in `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` can read **all** suites' results — including
   failing-row samples (`results.sample_failures`), the one place PII/PHI lands —
diff --git a/deploy/terraform/azure/sso.tf b/deploy/terraform/azure/sso.tf
index 8b67c0dc..ad010ab8 100644
--- a/deploy/terraform/azure/sso.tf
+++ b/deploy/terraform/azure/sso.tf
@@ -96,3 +96,18 @@ resource "azuread_application_pre_authorized" "spa_on_api" {
   authorized_client_id = azuread_application.spa.client_id
   permission_ids       = [random_uuid.api_scope.result]
 }
+
+# Pre-authorize the Microsoft Azure CLI (well-known first-party client id) on the
+# same scope, so operators can mint API bearers non-interactively for the live
+# smoke / MCP clients:
+#   az account get-access-token --resource api://<api-client-id>
+# Without this, the mint dies on AADSTS65001/650057 (the tenant can't dynamically
+# consent the CLI to a custom API). Mirrors the manual Graph PATCH applied
+# 2026-07-03 (W8 go-live smoke) so a future apply doesn't strip it — on first
+# apply, `terraform import` the existing grant instead of recreating it (see
+# deploy/README.md). Interim posture until ADR 0026 (DataQ-issued API keys).
+resource "azuread_application_pre_authorized" "azure_cli_on_api" {
+  application_id       = azuread_application.api.id
+  authorized_client_id = "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46" # Microsoft Azure CLI
+  permission_ids       = [random_uuid.api_scope.result]
+}

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ResolvedTarget:
    """The runner inputs a suite resolves to. ``table`` carries the file path for
    flat-file datasources; ``catalog`` is set only for Unity Catalog. ``batch`` is
    set only for a flat-file *batch* target, in which case ``table`` is empty until
    `materialize_path` lists the store and resolves the concrete path."""

    table: str
    schema: str | None
    catalog: str | None
    batch: BatchSpec | None = None


def resolve_target(conn_type: str, target: dict[str, Any] | None) -> ResolvedTarget:
    """Resolve ``target`` for a ``conn_type`` connection, or raise (422).

    Raises `SuiteTargetInvalidError` if the suite is targetless, the target is
    missing the field its datasource requires (`path` for flat files, `table`
    for SQL, `catalog` for Unity Catalog), or the connection type has no run path
    (orchestration providers — they are never suite datasources).
    """
    if not target:
        raise SuiteTargetInvalidError(
            "suite has no target configured", detail={"connection_type": conn_type}
        )

    if conn_type in _FLATFILE_TYPES:
        # A batch target (regex `pattern`) is resolved to a concrete path at run
        # time; a literal target carries the `path` directly. The two are mutually
        # exclusive — both set is an ambiguous target, not a silent batch win.
        if "pattern" in target and target.get("path"):
            raise SuiteTargetInvalidError(
                "flat-file target is ambiguous: set either 'path' (literal) or "
                "'pattern' (batch), not both",
                detail={"connection_type": conn_type},
            )
        if "pattern" in target:
            return ResolvedTarget(
                table="", schema=None, catalog=None, batch=_batch_spec(target, conn_type)
            )
        path = _require(target, "path", conn_type)
        return ResolvedTarget(table=path, schema=None, catalog=None)

    if conn_type == "snowflake":
        table = _require(target, "table", conn_type)
        return ResolvedTarget(table=table, schema=_str_or_none(target.get("schema")), catalog=None)

    if conn_type == "unity_catalog":
        table = _require(target, "table", conn_type)
        catalog = _require(target, "catalog", conn_type)
        return ResolvedTarget(
            table=table, schema=_str_or_none(target.get("schema")), catalog=catalog
        )

    raise SuiteTargetInvalidError(
        f"connection type {conn_type!r} has no run path (not a datasource)",
        detail={"connection_type": conn_type},
    )


def validate_target(conn_type: str, target: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """Write-time guard: a non-null target must resolve for its datasource.

    Reuses `resolve_target`'s rules so a target saved on a suite is always
    runnable. Callers only invoke this when a target is *provided* — a suite may
    be created/updated targetless (NULL), which is valid-but-not-yet-runnable.
    """
    resolve_target(conn_type, target)

Auth seam: DataQ-issued API keys / service tokens (REST + MCP) — provider-neutral identity

## Why

Today authentication is **exclusively Azure AD bearer tokens** (delegated/SSO) for both the REST API and `/mcp` — there is no DataQ-native credential. This is the **deepest remaining vendor lock-in** in the system and cuts against ADR [0010](../docs/adr/0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md) / [0013](../docs/adr/0013-marketplace-distribution-and-anti-lock-in.md): the `get_current_user` seam exists, but it has exactly *one* real implementation and the persistence layer is still Azure-shaped (`users.aad_object_id`). A BYOL customer on AWS/GCP (the ADR 0013 scenario) has no Azure AD and literally cannot authenticate.

It also closes the **programmatic-access gap**: headless agents / CI / always-on MCP clients want a long-lived, scoped, revocable secret — not a ~60-min Azure token they must refresh (see ADR [0008](../docs/adr/0008-mcp-server.md), which uses a token-validating `JWTVerifier`, not a client-driven OAuth provider).

## Scope — cross-cutting, NOT MCP-only

This is a **second authenticator behind the existing generic `get_current_user` seam** (ADR 0010), so the **REST API and `/mcp` accept it identically** — never build it for MCP alone. On MCP, fastmcp's `MultiAuth` lets `/mcp` accept *either* a DataQ key *or* an Azure token. Adding a second auth impl is also what finally *exercises* (validates) the seam.

## Recommended shape (phased)

1. **User-scoped PATs first** — a key belongs to a user and inherits their per-suite grants → **zero new authz model** (reuse the view/edit/admin ladder; optionally down-scope a key to read-only for MCP read tools / dashboards). ~80% of the value for a fraction of the change.
2. **Second authenticator behind the seam** — `Authorization: Bearer dq_live_…` → hash lookup → resolve the principal; else fall back to the Azure JWT. Shared by REST + MCP.
3. **Defer standalone service accounts** — they force the bigger move: generalize `users.aad_object_id` into a generic *principal* with pluggable identity bindings, and extend suite *sharing* to non-user principals. Sequence after PATs prove the seam.

## Security bar (credential surface — do not half-build)

- Hash-at-rest (argon2/bcrypt), **show-once** on creation, identifying prefix (`dq_live_…`), expiry defaults, revocation, last-used + audit.
- Hash lives in a **new `api_keys` table** — *not* the credential SecretStore (that's for retrievable connection secrets; a key hash is a verifier secret, never retrievable).
- **Lifecycle tied to the owner**: deactivating a user kills their keys (no SSO-policy backdoor outliving the account).
- Never log the key (only the prefix) — same discipline as the compliance posture (#436).

## Decision record

Direction captured in **ADR 0026** (Proposed) — auth-provider seam: second authenticator + the principal / identity-binding direction. Framed explicitly as discharging the identity-seam lock-in (ADR 0010/0013).

Post-v1, Theme 3 (Admin, access model & identity).

Good question on both — and the answer to the second is "nothing," so let me untangle them.

**The Databricks Free-Edition item — what the catch is**

You're right that it's test-harness-only; there's zero Free-Edition anything in the product code. The catch is purely in Databricks's terms: Free Edition is licensed **non-commercial use only**. Today that's fine — the deployed DataQ is a demo/eval environment. The checklist item exists only because the constraint is invisible: the live UC connection, Flow B of the smoke, and the trigger-bound `flow_b_medallion` DAG all quietly sit on a workspace whose ToS would be violated the day this deployment is used commercially (a paid pilot, a customer-facing demo tied to revenue, internal production use at a company). The "decision to record" is one honest paragraph, roughly: *"UC test env runs on Databricks Free Edition — acceptable while the deployment is demo/eval; any commercial use requires migrating the harness UC datasource to a paid workspace first."* Plus its operational corollaries you already know: no SLA, fair-use quota (compute can pause for the day mid-demo), and the three PATs expiring ~2026-09-30. It's a "write the line down so it isn't crossed by accident" item, not a defect.

**ADR 0026 — nothing is "going against" it, because it doesn't exist yet**

ADR 0026 is a *reserved number* — a proposed decision captured in [#461](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/461), not an accepted ADR anything could violate. The go-live checklist item is just: **make the call — build DataQ-issued API keys now, or defer to post-v1 — and record it.**

The substance: today the REST API and `/mcp` accept exactly one credential — an Azure AD user token. That's the deepest remaining vendor lock-in (a BYOL customer on AWS/GCP literally cannot authenticate, cutting against ADR 0010/0013), and it's why programmatic clients hurt: tokens die in ~60 minutes, and we had to pre-authorize the Azure CLI this afternoon just so the smoke could mint one non-interactively. #461's proposal is user-scoped PATs (`dq_live_…`, hashed at rest, show-once, revocable) as a second authenticator behind the existing `get_current_user` seam.

My recommendation: **defer to post-v1** (where it's already Theme 3). It's a credential surface with an explicit "do not half-build" security bar — wrong thing to rush in go-live week — and the CLI pre-auth (#565) plus MCP's Azure-token path cover v1's actual programmatic needs. The decision record would say exactly that, naming the pre-auth as the documented interim.

If you agree with both calls, I can land them as one small docs PR (progress.md go-live rows + a short ADR 0026 stub marking it Proposed/deferred with the rationale) — that clears two of the remaining checklist items in one go.

> AGENT

Good — both decisions made. Let me answer the design question first, then land everything as one docs PR.

**My recommendation: per-user PATs, and explicitly not basic auth**

- **Per-user PAT (phase 1 — the right start):** a key is created by a user, inherits that user's per-suite grants, so **zero new authz model** — the existing view/edit/admin ladder just works. Show-once on creation, hashed at rest (the DB stores a verifier, never the secret), identifying prefix (`dq_live_…`), expiry default, per-key revocation, last-used audit. It plugs in as a *second authenticator* behind the existing `get_current_user` seam, so REST and `/mcp` accept it identically with no route changes. This covers ~80% of the need: MCP clients, CI, headless agents acting for a person.

- **Basic auth — reject it.** DataQ has no password store today (identity is fully delegated to OIDC) — basic auth would force us to *become* a password system: storage, hashing policy, lockout, reset flows, credential-stuffing surface. And the credential itself is worse: one secret for the whole account (can't revoke a single integration without breaking all of them), no scoping, no expiry, replayed on every request, and routinely leaked via logs/proxies. A PAT gives the same ergonomics (`Authorization: Bearer …`) with none of that.

- **Service user / service accounts — phase 3, deliberately last.** The real need is automation that must *outlive a person* (owner offboards → their PATs die with them — which is the correct default, not a bug). But first-class service principals force the big move: generalizing `users.aad_object_id` into a generic principal with identity bindings, and extending suite *sharing* to non-user principals. Sequence that after PATs prove the seam. Interim escape hatch that costs nothing: a dedicated service Entra user (like `dataq-admin` today) owning automation keys.

So the ADR records: **PATs first → service principals later → basic auth never.** Now landing the docs. Checking the current go-live checklist and the post-v1 roadmap structure:

1	# ADR 0026 — DataQ-issued API keys / service tokens behind the auth seam (REST + MCP)
2	
3	- **Status:** Proposed
4	- **Date:** 2026-06-29
5	- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771
6	- **Related:** ADR [0010](0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md) (the `get_current_user` identity seam — Azure is one impl, not the architecture), [0013](0013-marketplace-distribution-and-anti-lock-in.md) (BYOL / anti-lock-in), [0008](0008-mcp-server.md) (MCP auth via `JWTVerifier` — bring-your-own-token today), [0020](0020-history-and-audit-strategy.md) (audit), compliance posture (#436)
7	- **Issue:** [#461](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/461)
8	
9	> **Stub — Proposed, not yet designed in full.** Captures the direction while it's fresh; to be fleshed out when Theme 3 (access/identity) is picked up post-v1.
10	
11	## Context
12	
13	Authentication today is **exclusively Azure AD bearer tokens** (delegated/SSO) for both the REST API and `/mcp`. There is no DataQ-native credential. Two problems follow:
14	
15	1. **Lock-in.** This is the deepest remaining Azure coupling. The `get_current_user` seam (ADR 0010) exists and service code never reads Entra claims (CLAUDE.md §11), but the seam has exactly *one* real implementation, and the persistence layer is still Azure-shaped (`users.aad_object_id`). A BYOL customer on AWS/GCP (ADR 0013) has no Azure AD and cannot authenticate at all.
16	2. **No programmatic access.** Headless agents, CI, and always-on MCP clients want a long-lived, scoped, revocable secret — not a ~60-min Azure token they must refresh (ADR 0008 uses a token-*validating* `JWTVerifier`, not a client-driven OAuth provider). There is no API-key / PAT / service-token mechanism.
17	
18	## Decision (direction — to be detailed)
19	
20	Introduce a **DataQ-issued credential as a second authenticator behind the existing `get_current_user` seam**, so the **REST API and `/mcp` accept it identically** — explicitly *not* an MCP-only feature. On MCP, fastmcp `MultiAuth` lets `/mcp` accept either a DataQ key or an Azure token. Adding a second real auth impl is also what *exercises* (and thereby validates) the seam ADR 0010 describes.
21	
22	**Phased:**
23	
24	1. **User-scoped PATs first.** A key belongs to a user and inherits that user's per-suite grants → **no new authz model** (reuse the `view < edit < admin < owner` ladder; optionally down-scope a key to read-only — ideal for MCP read tools / dashboards, smallest blast radius). ~80% of the value for a fraction of the change.
25	2. **Service-account principals later.** These force the larger move and should be sequenced after PATs prove the seam: generalize `users.aad_object_id` into a generic **principal** with pluggable identity bindings (Azure AD oid, API key, …), and extend suite **sharing** to non-user principals.
26	
27	**Credential bar (this is a new secret surface — not to be half-built):**
28	
29	- Hash-at-rest (argon2/bcrypt), **show-once** on creation, identifying prefix (`dq_live_…`), expiry defaults, revocation, last-used + audit.
30	- Hashes live in a **new `api_keys` table** — *not* the credential SecretStore (that store is for *retrievable* connection secrets; a key hash is a verifier secret, never retrievable).
31	- **Lifecycle tied to the owner**: deactivating a user kills their keys, so a PAT can't become an SSO-policy backdoor that outlives the account.
32	- Never logged (prefix only) — same discipline as the compliance posture (#436).
33	
34	## Consequences (anticipated)
35	
36	- Discharges the identity-seam lock-in (ADR 0010/0013): Azure AD becomes *one* authenticator behind the seam, not the only one — unblocking BYOL on non-Azure clouds.
37	- Closes the programmatic-access gap for REST automation and headless MCP clients without weakening the per-user authz model (PAT phase).
38	- Adds a credential-management surface (issue/list/revoke UI + API) and an audit obligation.
39	
40	## Open questions (for the full ADR)
41	
42	- Token format + verification cost (hash lookup on every request — caching?).
43	- Scope granularity: read-only vs read-write vs per-suite.
44	- Where service-account principals sit relative to the workspace-admin allowlist.
45	- Migration path for `users.aad_object_id` → generic principal without breaking existing ownership/shares.
46	
```

Rushing a PAT store into go-live week\nbuys little and risks the exact half-build this ADR warns against.\n\n**Shape confirmed** (evaluated against alternatives when the timing was decided):\n\n- **User-scoped PATs first** — as phased above. Inherits the per-suite ladder, zero new\n  authz model, revocable per-integration.\n- **Standalone service accounts later** — the real need is automation that outlives a person\n  (owner deactivated → their PATs correctly die), but first-class service principals force the\n  `users.aad_object_id` → generic-principal migration + non-user sharing; sequence after PATs.\n  Interim escape hatch: a dedicated service user (e.g. `dataq-admin`) owns automation keys.\n- **HTTP Basic auth — rejected.** DataQ has no password store (identity is delegated to OIDC);\n  Basic auth would make DataQ a password system (storage/hashing policy, lockout, reset flows,\n  credential-stuffing surface) for a *worse* credential: one secret per account (revoking one\n  integration breaks all), no scoping, no expiry, replayed on every request, and routinely\n  leaked via logs/proxies. A PAT has the same `Authorization`-header ergonomics without any\n  of that.\n\n## Consequences (anticipated)"
}

**The honest gaps (each mapped to where it's tracked):**

| # | Gap | Why it matters | Where tracked |
|---|---|---|---|
| G-a | **Monitors only what you remember to check** — hand-authored expectations; no anomaly baselines, no schema-drift, no auto-suggested checks. Category leaders' core pitch (Monte Carlo/Anomalo) is the inverse: automatic coverage. An unknown-unknown incident sails past DataQ. | Existential for "product"; the single biggest gap | **Theme 1** (remaining monitor kinds: `schema_drift`, `anomaly`) + **Theme 2** (auto-suggestion/LLM authoring) |
| G-b | **Scale unproven; structurally weak on 2 of 4 paths** — flat-file + UC runners load the whole file/table into worker pandas; largest table ever validated is a few thousand synthetic rows. No sampling/partition/incremental strategy for checks. (Snowflake pushes down via SQL — fine.) | 100M-row table = worker OOM; blocks any serious deployment | **Theme 7** (perf & scale — add: sampling/partition-aware/incremental check execution as a named workstream) |
| G-c | **Every "verified" is self-referential** — one operator, ~1 week live, against a harness built by the same author. Zero real-world data-pathology exposure at scale (schema churn, half-written files, encoding chaos in volume). | Unknown failure modes in the first real deployment | **Theme 10** (test-hardening) + first-real-workload milestone, post-v1 |
| G-d | **No incident workflow, no lineage, no ownership routing** — runs + alerts exist; "what broke downstream / who owns it / when was it resolved" doesn't. No data-access audit trail (the HIPAA gate). | This is what DQ products are bought for | **Theme 9** (results/reporting depth) + **Theme 4** / [#431](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/431) (audit trail); lineage/incident objects = new design doc needed |
| G-e | **Single-tenant, config-allowlist admin, one validated IdP** — fine internally, not sellable. | Blocks multi-team/commercial use | **Theme 3** (admin/access) + ADR 0026 / [#461](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/461) (API keys) |
| G-f | **Ecosystem: 4 datasources** vs the 30–50 a category product ships; no dbt integration (seam reserved); can't check the Postgres it runs on. | Adoption ceiling | **Theme 8** (datasource depth; generic-RDBMS adapter is the cheap first win) |
| G-g | **Engine risk: GX Core pin** — the product's core capability rides a fast-moving third party with documented API drift; DQX swap-in shape exists for UC only. | Strategic dependency | **Theme 2**'s engine-abstraction watch item (below) — no issue until the churn trigger fires |
| G-h | **Harness Databricks = Free Edition, non-commercial-only** — the UC demo leg cannot legally back a commercial demo, while ADR 0013's ambition is commercial BYOL. Trigger: before any commercial demo → paid workspace. | Licence landmine on the demo path | ADR 0021/0013 context — decision due **before any commercial demo** (also flagged in the local, untracked Week-8 working tracker) |

**Prioritisation signal for the post-v1 planner:** G-a and G-b are the two that change what the
product *is* (coverage-without-authoring + scale-safe execution); G-d is what makes it *usable in
anger* (incidents/lineage); the rest are adoption/positioning. Recommended post-v1 opening
sequence: Theme 1 `schema_drift` + `anomaly` (rides the ADR 0012 seam, no schema rewrite) →
scale-aware execution (G-b, Theme 7) → incident/lineage design doc (G-d).

> AGENT

Everything you asked for is in flight — here's the wrap-up:

**Your question, answered:** per-user **PATs** are the right implementation. They inherit the existing per-suite `view/edit/admin/owner` ladder (zero new authz model), are revocable per-integration, and slot in as a second authenticator behind the existing `get_current_user` seam so REST and `/mcp` accept them identically. **Service accounts** come later — they're only needed when automation must outlive a person, and they force the `aad_object_id` → generic-principal migration; until then a dedicated service user (like `dataq-admin`) owning keys covers it. **Basic auth is rejected outright** — DataQ has no password store today, and building one buys a strictly worse credential (unscoped, per-account, unrevocable per-integration, replayed on every request).

**Landed in PR [#566](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/566)** (docs-only, Week-8 milestone, CI running — I'll merge on green):
- **ADR 0026** now carries a decision record: deferred to post-v1 Theme 3, the PATs → service-principals phasing confirmed, Basic auth rejected with rationale, and the CLI pre-auth (#565) named as the v1 interim
- **Gap G-h** records the Free-Edition decision (demo/eval fine; paid workspace before any commercial use), and a new **gap G-i** captures your teardown note: Flows A/B/C, the 5 harness connections, demo users, and the seeded-breach check are all ADR-0021 test fixtures that must be stripped before any marketplace listing — mirrored as a `deploy/README.md` operational note so it's visible where deployments happen
- progress.md + CLAUDE.md checklists updated, and the **#177 epic** synced (all 29 boxes ticked + a status comment)

The go-live checklist is now down to two items: the **ops/renewals timers** (September credential cluster — this needs a decision from you on mechanism: calendar reminders vs. GitHub scheduled issues vs. something in-app) and the **`v1.0.0` tag + release notes + retro**.

> DEVELOPER

Since all the ops and renewal are tied to the demo environment, do we really need a reminder? We already have an note to tear them down. And once the azure deployment and features are finalized, we are going to publish the app and remove this demo instance altogether. what are you?

> AGENT

You're right — I agree we can drop the timers. My reasoning:

1. **Every expiring credential is demo-harness-scoped** (Snowflake PAT ~09-26, the three Databricks PATs ~09-30, the ADLS SAS in 2027). Nothing in the product or the repo depends on them; a customer deployment mints its own.

2. **Expiry is self-signaling — by DataQ itself.** When a PAT dies, connection tests and scheduled runs start failing, and the always-alert-on-operationally-failed-runs path (#419) fires. The platform literally monitors its own credential decay — you'll know within one 6-hour schedule cycle, which is a better reminder than any calendar entry.

3. **Recovery is cheap and documented.** Re-mint the PAT, update the readable-named KV secret — the procedure is in memory and the deploy notes. Worst case the demo is red for an hour; nothing is lost.

4. **The teardown note (G-i) already covers the end state.** If the demo instance is retired before September, the timers would have been pure noise anyway.

The only scenario a timer protects against is "you're demoing to someone important on Sept 27 and the Snowflake connection is red" — and given this is a portfolio/demo deployment, re-minting on failure is a perfectly acceptable posture.

So the decision to record: **ops/renewals timers consciously skipped — demo-scoped credentials, expiry self-signals through DataQ's own alerting, re-mint-on-failure is the documented recovery, and the instance is slated for teardown (G-i) before any commercial use.** That collapses the go-live checklist to a single item: **`v1.0.0` tag + release notes + retro**.

Rather than a standalone docs PR for one line, I'd fold this decision into the v1.0.0 close-out PR (which will touch progress.md and CLAUDE.md anyway, close epic #177 and the milestone, and declare v1 DONE). Want me to proceed with that — tag, release notes, retro, and this decision recorded in one final close-out?

def create_check(

    kind: str = "expectation",
    warn_threshold: float | None = None,

) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Add a new check (a Great Expectations expectation) to a suite.

    Use this for 'add a null check on email to the customer suite'. ``name`` is a
    human label; ``expectation_type`` is a GX expectation (e.g.
    ``expect_column_values_to_not_be_null``); ``config`` carries its arguments
    (e.g. ``{"column": "email"}``). Optional warn/fail/critical thresholds band
    the result severity. Requires edit access. Returns the created check's id.
    """
    sid = _parse_uuid(suite_id, field="suite_id")
    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
        require_permission(session, sid, user.id, minimum="edit")
        check = check_service.create_check(
            session,
            suite_id=sid,
            name=name,
            kind=kind,
            expectation_type=expectation_type,
            config=config or {},
            warn_threshold=Decimal(str(warn_threshold)) if warn_threshold is not None else None,
            fail_threshold=Decimal(str(fail_threshold)) if fail_threshold is not None else None,
            critical_threshold=(
                Decimal(str(critical_threshold)) if critical_threshold is not None else None
            ),
            actor_id=user.id,
        )

"""Adversarial-input fixtures + a JSON-safety contract for data-ingesting code.

Most of our bugs in data-handling code were *not* missing coverage — the lines
ran, just never with hostile data. A profiler/runner that eats arbitrary user
files has to survive columns it can't compare (mixed types), can't hash (nested
cells), or can't JSON-encode (NaN/Inf, bytes). This module centralises that
hostile-input set so any function that processes a DataFrame can be swept with
the same battery, and asserts the one contract that matters at the edge: the
output is **plain JSON** (no NaN/Inf, no exotic scalars) and never raised.

`ADVERSARIAL_FRAMES` is `(id, DataFrame)` pairs, each a single column named
``x``. Pass it to `pytest.mark.parametrize`. `assert_json_safe(value)` enforces
the JSON contract on any emitted scalar/structure.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import io
import json
from typing import Any

import pandas as pd


def _parquet_roundtrip(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Round-trip through Parquet with the Arrow backend the profiler/runner use.

    Arrow-backed columns raise *different* exception types than numpy ones (e.g.
    ``ArrowNotImplementedError`` vs ``TypeError``), so the Arrow variants are the
    ones that catch over-narrow ``except`` clauses.
    """
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    frame.to_parquet(buf)
    buf.seek(0)
    return pd.read_parquet(buf, dtype_backend="pyarrow")


ADVERSARIAL_FRAMES: list[tuple[str, pd.DataFrame]] = [
    # — object columns the numpy way —
    ("mixed_int_str", pd.DataFrame({"x": [10, "N/A", 20, "N/A"]})),
```

{
  "file_path": "/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/app/api/v1/_base.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"Shared request/response model base for the v1 API.\n\nEvery model in `backend/app/api/v1/` inherits `ApiModel` instead of Pydantic's\n`BaseModel` so cross-cutting input contracts live in exactly one place.\n\nThe one contract today: **no NUL (``\\\\x00``) anywhere in a payload** (#567).\nPydantic's `str` accepts NUL, but Postgres rejects it at INSERT time for both\ntext columns and JSONB — so a hostile/binary-contaminated string in any\npersisted free-text field (suite/check/connection names, descriptions, nested\ncheck ``config`` values, import documents …) would otherwise surface as a\ndriver ``ValueError`` → an unhandled 500 instead of a 422. Rejecting it at the\nvalidation boundary keeps the \"bad input is never a 500\" error-envelope\nguarantee and names the offending model in the standard validation error.\n\nThe walk runs on the *raw* inbound payload (``mode=\"before\"``), so nested\ndicts/lists — including dict *keys* — are covered before field parsing.\nResponse models constructed from ORM objects pass through untouched (the\nwalk only descends str/dict/list/tuple/set; DB data cannot contain NUL).\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nfrom typing import Any\n\nfrom pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator\n\n\ndef contains_nul(value: Any) -> bool:\n    \"\"\"True if a NUL (``\\\\x00``) appears in any string within ``value``\n    (recursing through dict keys/values and list/tuple/set items).\"\"\"\n    if isinstance(value, str):\n        return \"\\x00\" in value\n    if isinstance(value, dict):\n        return any(contains_nul(k) or contains_nul(v) for k, v in value.items())\n    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple, set, frozenset)):\n        return any(contains_nul(item) for item in value)\n    return False\n\n\nclass ApiModel(BaseModel):\n    \"\"\"`BaseModel` + the NUL-rejection contract (see module docstring).\"\"\"\n\n    @model_validator(mode=\"before\")\n    @classmethod\n    def _reject_nul_bytes(cls, data: Any) -> Any:\n        if contains_nul(data):\n            raise ValueError(\"NUL (\\\\x00) characters are not allowed\")\n        return data\n"
}

        app.dependency_overrides.clear()


def _suite_id(client: TestClient, db_session: Any, conn_type: str = "snowflake") -> str:
    """Create a connection (ORM) + suite (API) and return the suite id.

    `conn_type` lets a test pick the datasource (e.g. 's3' to exercise custom-SQL
    datasource gating); defaults to Snowflake.
    """
    owner = User(aad_object_id=uuid.uuid4().hex, email="owner@example.com")
    db_session.add(owner)
    db_session.flush()
    config = {"account": "ab12345.eu-west-1"} if conn_type == "snowflake" else {}
    conn = Connection(
        name=f"{conn_type}-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}",
        type=conn_type,
        env="dev",
        config=config,
        created_by=owner.id,
    )
    db_session.add(conn)
    db_session.commit()
    resp = client.post(
        "/api/v1/suites",
        json={"name": "finance", "description": None, "connection_id": str(conn.id)},
    )
    return str(resp.json()["id"])

{
  "file_path": "/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/tests/core/test_errors.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"`_jsonable` — the validation-envelope sanitizer (#371).\n\nPydantic's `exc.errors()` is not JSON-clean: `ctx` carries the live exception a\nmodel_validator raised and `input` echoes the raw payload. Before the fix, a\nmodel-validator `ValueError` made the 422 handler itself crash\n(`TypeError: Object of type ValueError is not JSON serializable` → 500). The\ncontract: whatever shape `errors()` takes, the result of `_jsonable` must\nsurvive `json.dumps` unchanged in structure, with plain scalars passed through\nand everything else stringified.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport json\nfrom typing import Any\n\nfrom backend.app.core.errors import _jsonable\n\n\ndef _dumps(value: Any) -> str:\n    return json.dumps(value)  # raises TypeError if anything non-JSON survives\n\n\ndef test_plain_scalars_pass_through() -> None:\n    for value in (None, \"s\", 7, 1.5, True):\n        assert _jsonable(value) == value\n    _dumps(_jsonable({\"a\": [1, \"x\", None, False]}))\n\n\ndef test_exception_object_in_ctx_is_stringified() -> None:\n    err = {\n        \"type\": \"value_error\",\n        \"loc\": (\"body\",),\n        \"msg\": \"Value error, NUL not allowed\",\n        \"input\": {\"name\": \"evil-\\x00\"},\n        \"ctx\": {\"error\": ValueError(\"NUL not allowed\")},\n    }\n    out = _jsonable([err])\n    _dumps(out)\n    assert out[0][\"ctx\"][\"error\"] == \"NUL not allowed\"\n    assert out[0][\"loc\"] == [\"body\"]  # tuple → list\n\n\ndef test_sets_and_nonstring_keys_are_coerced() -> None:\n    out = _jsonable({1: {\"s\": {frozenset({\"a\"})}}, \"b\": (2, 3)})\n    _dumps(out)\n    assert out[\"1\"][\"s\"] == [[\"a\"]]\n    assert out[\"b\"] == [2, 3]\n\n\ndef test_arbitrary_object_is_stringified() -> None:\n    class Weird:\n        def __str__(self) -> str:\n            return \"weird!\"\n\n    out = _jsonable({\"x\": Weird()})\n    _dumps(out)\n    assert out == {\"x\": \"weird!\"}\n"
}

Here's the diagnosis on #572:

**The CI failure is not the PR's fault — it's a flaky frontend test.** #572 is GitHub's CodeQL autofix for alert 24, and its entire diff is a backend test-file import-style cleanup (`test_auth.py` mixing `import ... as auth_mod` with a `from`-import of `_build_azure_scheme`; the fix routes everything through the alias). That can't break `SchedulesPanel.test.tsx > deletes a schedule after confirmation`, which is what failed — 1 of 334, and it passes 3/3 consecutive runs locally. Classic antd Popconfirm timing flake under jsdom on a slow CI runner.

name: Docs

# Build the MkDocs Material site and publish it to GitHub Pages (#288).
# Requires Pages enabled with Source = "GitHub Actions" (Settings → Pages) once.
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - docs/**
      - mkdocs.yml
      - requirements-docs.txt
      - .github/workflows/docs.yml
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# One in-flight Pages deployment at a time; don't cancel a publish mid-flight.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.13"
      - run: pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
      - run: mkdocs build --strict
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

  "content": "# DataQ v1.0.0 — retrospective\n\n> Internal document (excluded from the published site). Written 2026-07-04 at the\n> `v1.0.0` tag, closing the 8-week build (2026-05-24 → 2026-07-03). Every one of them later absorbed a change that would otherwise have\n  been a rewrite (DQX-shape UC runner, Slack/email publishers, freshness/volume\n  kinds, the generic-OIDC cutover).\n- **ADRs for anything with a rationale.** 27 short records; at least a dozen\n  \"why is it like this?\" moments during W7–W8 were answered by linking an ADR\n  instead of re-litigating. The decision-record pattern (0026's deferred-with-\n  shape-confirmed) works well for \"not now, but decided\".\n- **Adversarial testing as a standing rule (rule 4a).** The adversarial harness,\n  mutation spikes (mutmut 436/436 on `dashboard_service`; Stryker 82.35%), and\n  the qa-verifier agent's data-level batteries repeatedly caught what line\n  coverage could not — most recently the NUL-byte 500 (#567) at 98% coverage.\n- **The external live harness (ADR 0021).** Real Snowflake/UC/ADLS/ADF/Airflow\n  with seeded DQ issues turned \"works on my machine\" into three verified live\n  flows, and caught genuine production bugs (UC dialect regression #535,\n  credential leak in tracebacks #536, suite-delete cascade #540).\n\n## What hurt (do differently)\n\n- **Happy-path validation debt surfaced late.** The NUL-byte class (#567) and the\n  422-handler crash (#371) both lived in the gap between \"Pydantic accepts it\"\n  and \"Postgres refuses it\" — found in go-live week by the qa-verifier workout.\n  Lesson: run the data-level hostile battery *per feature PR* (it's cheap), not\n  only at milestones; the boundary between validation layers is where 500s hide.\n- **Deploy-day surprises cluster around identity/config, not code.** Celery beat\n  lock (#405), missing `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` for UAMI (#406), orphaned SWA EasyAuth\n  (#511), CLI consent (AADSTS65001/650057 → #565): none were app logic. The\n  start-time-secret-snapshot restart rule and the pre-authorized-client pattern\n  are now documented; budget explicit time for auth plumbing in any new cloud.\n- **Point-in-time counts in living docs rot fast.** progress.md/CLAUDE.md carry\n  counts that drifted within days (test totals, open-issue counts) and needed a\n  dedicated fact-check pass before the tag. Lesson: label point-in-time numbers\n  with their date (\"at flip\"), keep current-state counts in one place only.\n- **Session/token ergonomics taxed every live task.** SPA refresh tokens cap at\n  24h, az sessions are single-active-account, and every live verification began\n  with an auth dance. ADR 0026 (PATs) is deferred with eyes open — it should be\n  early in the post-v1 sequence if programmatic/live use grows.\n\n## Go-live decisions of record (2026-07-03/04)\n\n- **ADR 0026 (API keys): deferred to post-v1 Theme 3.** Shape confirmed —\n  user-scoped PATs first, service-account principals later, HTTP Basic auth\n  rejected. Interim: Azure CLI pre-authorized on the API scope (#565).\n- **Databricks Free Edition (gap G-h):** fine for demo/eval; migrate to a paid\n  workspace before any commercial use.\n- **Pre-marketplace harness teardown (gap G-i):** strip Flows A/B/C, the 5\n  harness connections, demo users, and the seeded-breach check from any\n  marketplace/customer-facing artifact.\n- **Ops/renewal timers: consciously skipped.** The September-2026 credential\n  cluster (Snowflake PAT ~09-26, Databricks PATs ×3 ~09-30, ADLS SAS 2027-06-28)\n  is demo-harness-scoped only; expiry self-signals through DataQ's own alerting\n  (#419 always-alerts operationally-failed runs) and recovery is re-mint +\n  KV update (documented).   "content": "# DataQ v1.0.0\n\nFirst stable release — a single-tenant data-quality monitoring platform built on Great Expectations (GX Core), delivered over an 8-week roadmap (2026-05-24 → 2026-07-03) and running in production on Azure Container Apps.\n\n## Highlights\n\n**Monitor 4 datasources.** Write expectation checks against Snowflake, ADLS Gen2 flat files, AWS S3 flat files, and Unity Catalog (Databricks) — all through one `ConnectionAdapter`/`CheckRunner` seam, with credentials held in Azure Key Vault and never returned by the API.\n\n**React to your pipelines.** Azure Data Factory and Apache Airflow integrate as orchestration providers (not datasources): near-real-time failure ingest via webhooks (shared-secret / HMAC-signed), trigger-on-success suite runs via provider-agnostic bindings, and a 10-minute polling fallback with gap recovery. A deliberate ADF failure was visible in DataQ 4m14s after firing.\n\n**Author checks like a product, not a config file.** Catalog-driven check editor with per-expectation forms, Monaco-backed custom SQL checks (read-only, single-statement, SQL-datasources only — ADR 0019), column profiler on all four datasources, dry-run preview, severity tiers (warn/fail/critical banding with thresholds-as-policy — ADR 0016), and freshness & volume monitor kinds beyond row-level expectations (ADR 0012).\n\n**Run and watch.** Async execution via Celery with live per-check progress, cancel, cron scheduling (DST-aware), run history with per-run outcome, a stuck-run reaper, and PII-minimising retention sweeps.\n\n**Know when it breaks.** Teams, Slack, and email alerting behind a `ResultPublisher` seam with severity-aware routing, dedup, per-check snooze suppression, and per-suite notification config. Operationally-failed runs always alert.\n\n**See it.** Monitoring dashboard (health score, trends, per-suite performance, period-over-period deltas), results explorer with drill-down to redacted failing-sample rows, and deep-linkable pages throughout.\n\n**Share it safely.** Suite-scoped sharing (view/edit/owner) with workspace-admin governance (ADR 0027) — verified live: unshared suites 404 (no existence leak), edit-tier cannot delete, `/admin` is 403 for non-admins.\n\n**Talk to it.** A FastMCP server exposes 8 curated tools at `/mcp` (same Azure AD token validation as REST, fail-closed) — verified end-to-end from a real VS Code MCP client config.\n\n**Deploy it anywhere (Azure today).** One cloud-neutral frontend image with runtime-injected generic OIDC config (`DATAQ_AUTH_*`, no MSAL), the API on internal ingress behind the frontend proxy, in-repo Terraform, GHCR images, and a validated GitHub Actions deploy pipeline. AWS/GCP IaC is on the post-v1 roadmap.\n\n## Quality bar\n\n- **1,289 backend tests, 98.4% line coverage** (CI-enforced gate ≥80%, includes the API layer)\n- **337 frontend tests, ~88% all-src line coverage** (CI gate ≥80%) + **25 Playwright E2E specs** in CI + an opt-in live-smoke lane\n- Adversarial-input harness + mutation-testing spikes (mutmut 436/436 killed on the spiked service; Stryker 82.35%)\n- Pre-tag QA: a hostile data-level workout against the running app (found and fixed the one blocker — NUL-byte input now a structured 422 everywhere), live cross-user authz verification as a non-admin user (15/15), and live webhook-auth hostility probes (7/7 structured 401s)\n- 12 required CI checks: Ruff, Black, mypy (app+tests), pytest, frontend lint/format/test/E2E, secret scanning, Bandit, CodeQL, pip-audit/pnpm-audit CVE gates (zero ignored advisories)\n\n## Documentation\n\n- User guides + reference: https://theurgicduke771.github.io/DataQ/ (getting started, concepts, datasources & checks, scheduling, orchestration, notifications, MCP setup, best practices, feature matrix, runbook)\n- 27 Architecture Decision Records in `docs/adr/`\n- Deployment guide with a complete environment-variable reference in `deploy/`\n\n## Known deferrals (decided, not forgotten)\n\n- DataQ-issued API keys / service tokens — deferred to post-v1 with the shape confirmed (user-scoped PATs first; HTTP Basic auth rejected) — ADR 0026\n- The live demo environment runs on Databricks Free Edition (non-commercial); it and all demo fixtures are slated for teardown before any commercial/marketplace use\n- Full post-v1 backlog: 50 issues across 13 themes in `context/post-v1-roadmap.md`\n\n## Stats\n\n405 commits · ~570 PRs+issues · 27 ADRs · 8 weeks · roadmap 187/189 (2 items consciously re-scoped to post-v1)\n"

  "content": "# DataQ v1.0.0\n\nFirst stable release — a single-tenant data-quality monitoring platform built on Great Expectations (GX Core), delivered over an 8-week roadmap (2026-05-24 → 2026-07-03) and running in production on Azure Container Apps.\n\n## Highlights\n\n**Monitor 4 datasources.** Write expectation checks against Snowflake, ADLS Gen2 flat files, AWS S3 flat files, and Unity Catalog (Databricks) — all through one `ConnectionAdapter`/`CheckRunner` seam, with credentials held in Azure Key Vault and never returned by the API.\n\n**React to your pipelines.** Azure Data Factory and Apache Airflow integrate as orchestration providers (not datasources): near-real-time failure ingest via webhooks (shared-secret / HMAC-signed), trigger-on-success suite runs via provider-agnostic bindings, and a 10-minute polling fallback with gap recovery. A deliberate ADF failure was visible in DataQ 4m14s after firing.\n\n**Author checks like a product, not a config file.** Catalog-driven check editor with per-expectation forms, Monaco-backed custom SQL checks (read-only, single-statement, SQL-datasources only — ADR 0019), column profiler on all four datasources, dry-run preview, severity tiers (warn/fail/critical banding with thresholds-as-policy — ADR 0016), and freshness & volume monitor kinds beyond row-level expectations (ADR 0012).\n\n**Run and watch.** Async execution via Celery with live per-check progress, cancel, cron scheduling (DST-aware), run history with per-run outcome, a stuck-run reaper, and PII-minimising retention sweeps.\n\n**Know when it breaks.** Teams, Slack, and email alerting behind a `ResultPublisher` seam with severity-aware routing, dedup, per-check snooze suppression, and per-suite notification config. Operationally-failed runs always alert.\n\n**See it.** Monitoring dashboard (health score, trends, per-suite performance, period-over-period deltas), results explorer with drill-down to redacted failing-sample rows, and deep-linkable pages throughout.\n\n**Share it safely.** Suite-scoped sharing (view/edit/owner) with workspace-admin governance (ADR 0027) — verified live: unshared suites 404 (no existence leak), edit-tier cannot delete, `/admin` is 403 for non-admins.\n\n**Talk to it.** A FastMCP server exposes 8 curated tools at `/mcp` (same Azure AD token validation as REST, fail-closed) — verified end-to-end from a real VS Code MCP client config.\n\n**Deploy it anywhere (Azure today).** One cloud-neutral frontend image with runtime-injected generic OIDC config (`DATAQ_AUTH_*`, no MSAL), the API on internal ingress behind the frontend proxy, in-repo Terraform, GHCR images, and a validated GitHub Actions deploy pipeline. AWS/GCP IaC is on the post-v1 roadmap.\n\n## Quality bar\n\n- **1,289 backend tests, 98.4% line coverage** (CI-enforced gate ≥80%, includes the API layer)\n- **337 frontend tests, ~88% all-src line coverage** (CI gate ≥80%) + **25 Playwright E2E specs** in CI + an opt-in live-smoke lane\n- Adversarial-input harness + mutation-testing spikes (mutmut 436/436 killed on the spiked service; Stryker 82.35%)\n- Pre-tag QA: a hostile data-level workout against the running app (found and fixed the one blocker — NUL-byte input now a structured 422 everywhere), live cross-user authz verification as a non-admin user (15/15), and live webhook-auth hostility probes (7/7 structured 401s)\n- 12 required CI checks: Ruff, Black, mypy (app+tests), pytest, frontend lint/format/test/E2E, secret scanning, Bandit, CodeQL, pip-audit/pnpm-audit CVE gates (zero ignored advisories)\n\n## Documentation\n\n- User guides + reference: https://theurgicduke771.github.io/DataQ/ (getting started, concepts, datasources & checks, scheduling, orchestration, notifications, MCP setup, best practices, feature matrix, runbook)\n- 27 Architecture Decision Records in `docs/adr/`\n- Deployment guide with a complete environment-variable reference in `deploy/`\n\n## Known deferrals (decided, not forgotten)\n\n- DataQ-issued API keys / service tokens — deferred to post-v1 with the shape confirmed (user-scoped PATs first; HTTP Basic auth rejected) — ADR 0026\n- The live demo environment runs on Databricks Free Edition (non-commercial); it and all demo fixtures are slated for teardown before any commercial/marketplace use\n- Full post-v1 backlog: 50 issues across 13 themes in `context/post-v1-roadmap.md`\n\n## Stats\n\n405 commits · ~570 PRs+issues · 27 ADRs · 8 weeks · roadmap 187/189 (2 items consciously re-scoped to post-v1)\n"

{"results":[{"title":"Connect and query Azure HorizonDB (Preview)","content":"# Connect and query Azure HorizonDB (Preview)\nAzure HorizonDB is Azure's next-generation PostgreSQL platform, designed to let developers securely connect to an Azure HorizonDB cluster and run standard PostgreSQL read and write queries without changing application code. Applications connect to a primary (read-write) endpoint for transactional workloads and administrative operations, or to read-only endpoints to scale read traffic across multiple readable replicas. Azure HorizonDB is fully compatible with existing PostgreSQL clients, drivers, ORMs, and SQL syntax, allowing developers to integrate it into current applications with minimal or no code changes.\nApplications can connect using standard PostgreSQL connection strings to either the primary cluster endpoint for read-write workloads or the read-replica endpoint for read-only traffic.\nYou can find Azure HorizonDB cluster endpoint details in the **Overview** page:\n[![Screenshot showing the Overview page and connection details.](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/connectivity/media/how-to-connect-query-guide/overview.png)](media/how-to-connect-query-guide/overview.png#lightbox)\nHow to connect to Azure HorizonDB read/write instance (primary endpoint):\n`psql \"host=<Azure HorizonDB-primary-endpoint> port=5432 dbname=<database_name> user=<username> sslmode=require\"`\nHow to connect to Azure HorizonDB read replica pool (reader endpoint):\n`psql \"host=<Azure HorizonDB-reader-endpoint> port=5432 dbname=<database_name> user=<username> sslmode=require\"`\nThis guide also includes TLS recommendations and extensions that you can use to connect to the server in supported languages below.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/connectivity/how-to-connect-query-guide"},{"title":"Develop AI apps with LangChain for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)","content":"# Develop AI apps with LangChain for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)\n[LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/) is a large language model (LLM) orchestration framework that simplifies building generative AI applications. No special configuration is necessary but do enforce TLS 1.2 for newly created servers. We recommend if you're using TLS 1.0 and 1.1, then you update the TLS version for your servers. See [Connect clients with TLS security to your database in Azure HorizonDB (Preview)](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/security/security-tls-how-to-connect).\n## PostgreSQL extensions\nAzure HorizonDB supports PostgreSQL extensions to add extra functionality to your database. Extensions are packages of related SQL objects that you can load or remove with a single command.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/connectivity/how-to-connect-query-guide#quickstarts"},{"title":"High availability for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)","content":"# High availability for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)\n## Failover process\nAzure HorizonDB guarantees that committed transactions aren't lost during failover. The WAL service persists every committed transaction durably across zones before acknowledging it to the client. Because all replicas read from the same durable storage, the promoted standby has access to every committed write.\nTransactions that are in progress but not yet committed at the time of failover are rolled back, consistent with standard PostgreSQL ACID behavior.\n## Application considerations\nTo get the most out of high availability in Azure HorizonDB, consider the following application-level practices:\n1. **Implement connection retry logic** - Use exponential backoff with retry on transient connection errors. Most PostgreSQL client libraries and frameworks support automatic retry configuration.\n2. **Use endpoints** - Always connect through the read-write or read-only endpoints rather than directly to specific replicas. The endpoints automatically route to the correct replica after a failover.\n3. **Avoid long-running transactions** - Long transactions delay planned failover completion and increase the risk of rollback during unplanned failover.\n4. **Don't store state in temporary tablespaces** - Temporary objects don't persist across failover events. Avoid creating user schema objects in temporary tablespaces.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/high-availability/concepts-high-availability-failover#failover-process"},{"title":"Implement AI pipelines for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)","content":"# Implement AI pipelines for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)\n## Monitor pipelines in Visual Studio Code\nThe PostgreSQL extension for Visual Studio Code includes a **Pipelines & Workflows** view where you can inspect AI pipeline runs and monitor execution state without leaving your editor.\n### Open the Pipelines pane\n1. In Visual Studio Code, open the PostgreSQL extension.\n2. In **Object Explorer**, right-click your database.\n3. Select **Pipelines & Workflows**.\n4. Select the **AI Pipelines** tab.\n[![Screenshot of the AI Pipelines tab in the PostgreSQL extension for Visual Studio Code showing pipeline definitions, runs, and the pipeline graph.](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/ai/media/pipelines/ai-pipeline-usage.png)](media/pipelines/ai-pipeline-usage.png#lightbox)\n### Understand the pipeline graph\nWhen you select a pipeline run, the center pane displays the execution graph with color-coded step types:\n1. **Blue**: Source and sink steps (data entry and exit points).\n2. **Green**: Intermediate processing steps (chunk, embed, extract, generate, rank operations).\n3. **Pink**: External calls (model API calls and external services).\nUse this color mapping to quickly validate that your pipeline is shaped correctly and executing as expected.\n### Inspect run details\nFor each pipeline run, you can verify:\n1. **Status**: `completed`, `running`, or `failed`.\n2. **Run ID**: Unique identifier for traceability.\n3. **Start time and duration**: Performance insights.\n4. **Pipeline definition link**: Navigate from a run back to its definition to review recent changes.\nIf a run fails, open the graph view and inspect the step where execution stopped to identify the issue.\n## Limitations during preview\n1. Sources are HorizonDB tables. To ingest from blob storage or external systems, land the content in a staging table first; the pipeline handles chunking, embedding, checkpointing, and sink writes from there.\n2. Pipelines run on the primary. Read replicas can query `ai.*` views but don't execute pipelines.\n3. Pipeline state isn't portable across major versions of `pg_durable` during **preview**. Drain or pause running pipelines before upgrading.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/ai/ai-pipelines#monitor-pipelines-in-visual-studio-code"},{"title":"Quickstart: Use Java and JDBC for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)","content":"# Quickstart: Use Java and JDBC for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)\n## Create an Azure HorizonDB cluster\n```bash\npsql \"REDACTED" < create_user.sql\n```\nNow, run the following command to delete the temporary SQL script file:\n```bash\nrm create_user.sql\n```\n### Create a new Java project\nUsing your favorite IDE, create a new Java project by using Java 8 or later. Add a *pom.xml* file in the root directory with the following contents:\nThis file is an [Apache Maven](https://maven.apache.org/) file that configures your project to use:\n1. Java 8\n2. A recent PostgreSQL driver for Java\n### Prepare a configuration file to connect to Azure HorizonDB\nCreate a *src/main/resources/application.properties* file, and add the following contents:\n```bash\ncat << EOF > src/main/resources/application.properties\nurl=jdbc:postgresql://${AZ_HORIZONDB_FQDN}:5432/${AZ_DATABASE_NAME}?sslmode=require\nuser=${AZ_POSTGRESQL_NON_ADMIN_USERNAME}\npassword=${AZ_POSTGRESQL_NON_ADMIN_PASSWORD}\nEOF\n```\nNote\nThe configuration property `url` includes `?sslmode=require` to ensure that the JDBC driver uses TLS (Transport Layer Security) when connecting to the database. Azure HorizonDB requires TLS, and it's a recommended security practice.\n### Create a SQL file to generate the database schema\nUse a *src/main/resources/schema.sql* file to create a database schema. Create that file with the following content:\n```sql\nDROP TABLE IF EXISTS todo;\nCREATE TABLE todo (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, description text, details text, done BOOLEAN);\n```","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/connectivity/connect-java#create-an-azure-horizondb-cluster"},{"title":"What is Azure HorizonDB (Preview)?","content":"# What is Azure HorizonDB (Preview)?\nAzure HorizonDB is a cloud native fully managed, AI-ready database service built on PostgreSQL. It combines a disaggregated compute and storage architecture with a database-as-a-log design to deliver predictable performance, enterprise-grade security, high availability, and seamless scalability for mission-critical workloads.\nAzure HorizonDB empowers developers to build intelligent, AI-powered applications through native support for vector embeddings and integration with Azure AI Foundry Tools, while retaining full PostgreSQL compatibility so existing applications can easily migrate to Azure HorizonDB.\n## Azure HorizonDB use cases\nAzure HorizonDB is a cloud native scalable alternative to self-managed PostgreSQL and is designed for mission-critical workloads not limited to but including:\n1. **Transactional workloads (OLTP)** - High-throughput, low-latency transaction processing with predictable performance for line-of-business applications, e-commerce platforms, and SaaS backends.\n2. **AI and intelligent applications** - Native vector search and embedding support lets you build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, recommendation engines, and semantic search directly within the database layer. AI model management and AI pipelines further simplify building intelligent applications within the database.\n3. **Massive read scale-out** - Applications that can benefit from read scale-out with shared zone resilient data.\n4. **Hybrid applications** - Integration with Azure ecosystem, mirror transactional data to Fabric One lake integrating with other analytical data.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/overview"},{"title":"What is the PostgreSQL extension for Visual Studio Code? (Preview)","content":"# What is the PostgreSQL extension for Visual Studio Code? (Preview)\nThe PostgreSQL extension for Visual Studio Code simplifies PostgreSQL database management and development. You can connect to PostgreSQL databases, write and execute queries, and manage database objects without leaving Visual Studio Code.\nThe extension integrates with Azure-managed PostgreSQL services, including:\n1. **Azure HorizonDB** - a cloud-native PostgreSQL service built for tier-1 enterprise workloads. HorizonDB features a disaggregated storage/compute architecture, low-latency commits, fast failover, load-balanced read scale-out across readable HA replicas, and deep AI integration.\nThe same extension works against both services. Where behavior differs (for example, connection endpoints or supported authentication methods), it's called out in the sections that follow.\n## How to install the extension\nYou can install the PostgreSQL extension directly from the Extensions Marketplace in Visual Studio Code. Follow these steps:\n1. Open the Extensions view in Visual Studio Code by selecting the **Extensions** icon in the Activity Bar or by using the **View: Extensions** command.\n2. Search for **PostgreSQL** in the Extensions Marketplace.\n3. Select the **PostgreSQL** extension authored by Microsoft and select **Install**.\nWhen you install the extension, an elephant icon appears to represent the PostgreSQL page in the Visual Studio Code sidebar.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/development/vs-code-extension/vs-code-overview"},{"title":"List of extensions and modules by version of PostgreSQL for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)","content":"# List of extensions and modules by version of PostgreSQL for Azure HorizonDB (Preview)\n| **Extension or module** | **Version** | **Notes**| \n|  --- | --- | ---  |\n| [pg_prewarm](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgprewarm.html) prewarms the cache with relation data. | 1.2 ^\\*^ | ^\\*^ Enable corresponding libraries in the `shared_preload_libraries` parameter.Read the special considerations for extension [pg_prewarm](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/extensions/concepts-extensions-considerations#pg_prewarm) in Azure HorizonDB. |\n| [pg_repack](https://reorg.github.io/pg_repack/) reorganizes tables in PostgreSQL databases with minimal locks. | 1.5.1 | Read the special considerations for extension [pg_repack](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/extensions/concepts-extensions-considerations#pg_repack) in Azure HorizonDB. |\n| [pgrowlocks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgrowlocks.html) shows row-level locking information. | 1.2 |  |\n| [pg_stat_statements](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgstatstatements.html) tracks execution statistics of all SQL statements executed. | 1.11 ^\\*^ | ^\\*^ Enable corresponding libraries in the `shared_preload_libraries` parameter.Read the special considerations for extension [pg_stat_statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/extensions/concepts-extensions-considerations#pg_stat_statements) in Azure HorizonDB. |\n| [pgstattuple](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgstattuple.html) shows tuple-level statistics. | 1.5 | Read the special considerations for extension [pgstattuple](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/horizondb/extensions/concepts-extensions-considerations#pgstattuple) in Azure HorizonDB. |\n| [pg_trgm](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgtrgm.html) provides text similarity measurement and index searching based on trigrams. | 1.6 |
