{"results":[{"title":"Connect to your SQL database in Microsoft Fabric","content":"# Connect to your SQL database in Microsoft Fabric\n## Find SQL connection string\nIn Microsoft Fabric, the SQL analytics endpoint and SQL database are accessible through a Tabular Data Stream, or TDS endpoint, familiar to all modern web applications that interact with [a SQL Server TDS endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/networking/tds-8). This is referred to as the SQL connection string within the Microsoft Fabric user interface.\n1. The server name of the SQL database is similar to the server name of Azure SQL Database, `<server-unique-identifier>.database.windows.net`.\n2. The SQL analytics endpoint server name is similar to the server name of a warehouse, `<server-unique-identifier>.<tenant>.fabric.microsoft.com`.\nTo find the server name for your **Fabric SQL database**:\n1. Go to the settings of your SQL database item.\n2. Or, in the item list, select the `...` menu. Select **Settings** then **Connection strings**. Fabric provides complete connection strings for providers including ADO.NET, JDBC, ODBC, PHP, and Go.\n3. Or, select the **Open in** button and select **SQL Server Management Studio** or **Visual Studio Code**. The server name and database name are displayed.\nTo find the server name of the **SQL analytics endpoint** of your SQL database:\n1. Go to the settings of your SQL database item, then select **Connection strings**.\n2. Or, select the `...` menu, then select **SQL endpoint**, then copy the **SQL connection string**. This is the server name.\n## Open in button to connect\nYou can easy connect to your SQL database with the **Open in** button in the Fabric portal [query editor](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/database/sql/query-editor). Choose [SQL Server Management Studio](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/ssms/download-sql-server-management-studio-ssms) or [the MSSQL extension for Visual Studio Code](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/tools/visual-studio-code/mssql-extensions?view=fabric-sqldb&preserve-view=true).\n[![Screenshot from the Fabric portal query editor showing the Open in button for easy connections with SSMS or the MSSQL extension in VS Code.](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/database/sql/media/connect/open-in-sql-tools.png)](media/connect/open-in-sql-tools.png#lightbox)","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/database/sql/connect#find-sql-connection-string"},{"title":"Warehouse connectivity","content":"# Warehouse connectivity\n**Applies to:** ✅ SQL analytics endpoint and Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric\nIn Microsoft Fabric, users access a SQL analytics endpoint or Warehouse through a Tabular Data Stream (TDS) endpoint. Modern web applications interact with [a SQL Server TDS endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/networking/tds-8). Within Microsoft Fabric settings, this endpoint is labeled as the **SQL connection string**.\nTip\nFor a tutorial on connecting with common tools, see [Connect to Fabric Data Warehouse](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/how-to-connect).\n## Authentication to warehouses in Fabric\nIn Microsoft Fabric, the SQL connection string supports two types of authenticated users:\n1. Microsoft Entra ID user principals, or user identities\n2. Microsoft Entra ID service principals\nFor more information, see [Microsoft Entra authentication as an alternative to SQL authentication in Microsoft Fabric](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/entra-id-authentication).\nThe SQL connection string requires TCP port 1433 to be open. TCP 1433 is the standard SQL Server port number. The SQL connection string also respects the Warehouse or Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint security model for data access. Users can access data for all objects to which they have permission.\nFor more information about security in the SQL analytics endpoint, see [OneLake security for SQL analytics endpoints](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/onelake/sql-analytics-endpoint-onelake-security).","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/connectivity"},{"title":"Connect to Fabric Data Warehouse","content":"# Connect to Fabric Data Warehouse\n## Connect using dbt\nThe `dbt` adapter is a data transformation framework that uses software engineering best practices like testing and version control to reduce code, automate dependency management, and ship more reliable data—all with SQL.\nThe `dbt` data platform-specific adapter plugins allow users to connect to the data store of choice. To connect to a warehouse from `dbt`, use `dbt-fabric` adapter. Similarly, the Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pool data source has its own adapter, `dbt-synapse`.\nBoth adapters support Microsoft Entra ID authentication and allow developers to use `az cli authentication`. However, SQL authentication isn't supported for `dbt-fabric`.\nThe `dbt` Fabric DW Adapter uses the `pyodbc` library to establish connectivity with the Warehouse. The `pyodbc` library is an ODBC implementation in Python language that uses [Python Database API Specification v2.0](https://peps.python.org/pep-0249/). The `pyodbc` library directly passes connection string to the database driver through SQLDriverConnect in the `msodbc` connection structure to Microsoft Fabric using a TDS (Tabular Data Streaming) proxy service.\nFor more information, see the following resources:\n1. [Connect Microsoft Fabric](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/cloud/connect-data-platform/connect-microsoft-fabric) to connect in dbt Cloud.\n2. [Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse dbt adapter setup](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/core/connect-data-platform/fabric-setup) to connect with dbt Core.\n3. [Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse dbt adapter configuration](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/fabric-configs) for additional configuration details.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/how-to-connect#connect-using-dbt"},{"title":"Connect to Fabric Data Warehouse","content":"# Connect to Fabric Data Warehouse\n## Connectivity by other means\nAny non-Microsoft tool can also use the SQL connection string via ODBC or OLE DB drivers to connect to a Microsoft Fabric Warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint, using Microsoft Entra ID authentication. For more information and sample connection strings, see [Microsoft Entra authentication as an alternative to SQL authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/entra-id-authentication).\n### Custom applications\nIn Microsoft Fabric, a Warehouse and a Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint provide a SQL connection string. Data is accessible from a vast ecosystem of SQL tooling, provided they can authenticate using Microsoft Entra ID. For more information, see [Connection libraries for Microsoft SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/sql-connection-libraries#drivers-for-relational-access). For more information and sample connection strings, see [Microsoft Entra authentication as an alternative to SQL authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/entra-id-authentication).","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/how-to-connect#connectivity-by-other-means"},{"title":"Connect to Fabric Data Warehouse","content":"# Connect to Fabric Data Warehouse\n**Applies to:** ✅ SQL analytics endpoint and Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric\nThis tutorial covers connecting tools and applications to your SQL analytics endpoint or Warehouse, or to the snapshot of a Warehouse.\nTo get started, you need access to a [SQL analytics endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-engineering/lakehouse-overview) or a [Warehouse](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/data-warehousing) within a workspace with **Contributor** or higher permissions.\n## Find the warehouse connection string\nTo find the server name of your warehouse item:\n1. Open the **Settings** of your warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint.\n2. In the **Settings** window, select the **SQL endpoint** page.\n3. Copy the **SQL connection string** and use it to connect externally to the item from Power BI desktop, applications, or client tools. This is the server name of your warehouse.\n4. You should provide the warehouse item name as the **Initial Catalog** or **Database name** when you connect. If you don't provide [the `InitialCatalog` connection string property](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/connectivity#connection-behavior-for-initialcatalog), your initial connection context will be to the `master` warehouse.\n ![Screenshot from the Fabric portal of the Settings window, SQL endpoint page.](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/media/how-to-connect/connection-string.png)","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/how-to-connect"},{"title":"What is the SQL analytics endpoint for a SQL database in Fabric?","content":"# What is the SQL analytics endpoint for a SQL database in Fabric?\n## Connect to the SQL analytics endpoint\nYou can connect to the SQL analytics endpoint via Power BI desktop or client tools such as [SQL Server Management Studio](https://aka.ms/ssms) or [the MSSQL extension for Visual Studio Code](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/tools/visual-studio-code-extensions/mssql/mssql-extension-visual-studio-code). The SQL analytics endpoint connection string looks like `<server-unique-identifier>.<tenant>.fabric.microsoft.com` as opposed to the connection string of the SQL database itself, which looks like `<server-unique-identifier>.database.windows.net`. To find the connection string of the SQL analytics endpoint in the workspace, select the `...` menu and then **Copy SQL connection string**, or find the connection string in **Settings** in the **SQL endpoint** page.\nYou can also query the SQL analytics endpoint in the [SQL query editor in the Fabric portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/database/sql/query-editor) by selecting the **SQL analytics endpoint** from drop-down list, as shown in the following screenshot:\n![Screenshot from the Fabric portal of the drop-down list selector of SQL database or SQL analytics endpoint.](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/database/sql/media/sql-analytics-endpoint/sql-analytics-endpoint-selector.png)\nFor more information on connecting to your SQL database data, see [Connect to your SQL database in Microsoft Fabric](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/database/sql/connect).\n## Access control using SQL security\nYou can set object-level security for database users or database roles using ([workspace roles](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/database/sql/authorization#workspace-roles) or [item permissions](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/database/sql/authorization#item-permissions)) in the Fabric portal, or by using [GRANT](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/grant-transact-sql?view=fabric-sqldb&preserve-view=true), [REVOKE](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/revoke-transact-sql?view=fabric-sqldb&preserve-view=true), and [DENY](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/deny-transact-sql?view=fabric-sqldb&preserve-view=true) Transact-SQL statements. These security rules will only apply for accessing data via SQL analytics endpoint.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/database/sql/sql-analytics-endpoint#connect-to-the-sql-analytics-endpoint"},{"title":"sql_endpoint Package-Functions","content":"# sql\\_endpoint Package\r\n\r\nSQL endpoint module for Microsoft Fabric.\r\n\r\nThis module provides functions to discover Fabric SQL endpoints, retrieve their connection strings, and refresh their metadata.\r\n\r\n## Functions\r\n\r\n### get\\_sql\\_endpoint\\_connection\\_string\r\n\r\nGet the SQL endpoint connection string of the specified warehouse.\r\n\r\nNote\r\n\r\nThis function wraps the Fabric REST API [Items - Get Connection String](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/fabric/sqlendpoint/items/get-connection-string).\r\n\r\n```python\r\nget_sql_endpoint_connection_string(warehouse: str | UUID | None = None, warehouse_type: Literal['Lakehouse', 'MirroredDatabase'] | None = None, sql_endpoint_id: str | UUID | None = None, *, workspace: str | UUID | None = None, guest_tenant_id: str | None = None, private_link_type: str | None = None, credential: TokenCredential | None = None) -> str\r\n```\r\n\r\n#### Parameters\r\n\r\n| Name | Description |\r\n| --- | --- |\r\n| warehouse | [str](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str) or [UUID](https://docs.python.org/3/library/uuid.html#uuid.UUID)<br><br>The name or ID of the warehouse. Mutually exclusive with *sql\\_endpoint\\_id*.<br><br>Default value: None |\r\n| warehouse\\_type | &lt;xref:Literal&gt;[&lt;xref:`”Lakehouse”, `\"MirroredDatabase\"] <br><br>The type of the warehouse. Must be provided if *warehouse* is provided. Mutually exclusive with *sql\\_endpoint\\_id*.<br><br>Default value: None |\r\n| sql\\_endpoint\\_id | [str](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str) or [UUID](https://docs.python.org/3/library/uuid.html#uuid.UUID)<br><br>The SQL endpoint ID. Mutually exclusive with *warehouse* and *warehouse\\_type*.<br><br>Default value: None |\r\n| workspace | [str](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str) or [UUID](https://docs.python.org/3/library/uuid.html#uuid.UUID)<br><br>The Fabric workspace name or UUID object containing the workspace ID. Defaults to None which resolves to the workspace of the attached lakehouse or if no lakehouse attached, resolves to the workspace of the notebook.<br><br>Default value: None |\r\n| guest\\_tenant\\_id | [str](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str)<br><br>The guest tenant ID to use for cross-tenant access scenarios.<br><br>Default value: None |\r\n| private\\_link\\_type | [str](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str)<br><br>The private link type to use for the connection string.<br><br>Default value: None |\r\n| credential | &lt;xref:sempy.fabric.sql\\_endpoint.TokenCredential&gt;<br><br>The credential for token acquisition. Must be an instance of [azure.core.credentials.TokenCredential](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/python/sdk/authentication/overview). If None, the default credential will be used.<br><br>Default value: None |\r\n\r\n#### Keyword-Only Parameters\r\n\r\n| Name | Description |\r\n| --- | --- |\r\n| workspace | Default value: None |\r\n| guest\\_tenant\\_id | Default value: None |\r\n| private\\_link\\_type | Default value: None |\r\n| credential | Default value: None |\r\n\r\n#### Returns\r\n\r\n| Type | Description |\r\n| --- | --- |\r\n| [str](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str) | The SQL endpoint connection string of the specified warehouse. |","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/python/api/semantic-link-sempy/sempy.fabric.sql_endpoint?view=semantic-link-python"},{"title":"Query the warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint","content":"# Query the warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint\n**Applies to:** ✅ [SQL analytics endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/data-warehousing#data-warehousing-items), [Warehouse](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/data-warehousing#fabric-data-warehouse), and [Mirrored Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/mirroring/overview) in Microsoft Fabric\nIn this article, learn how to query a warehouse or a SQL analytics endpoint in Microsoft Fabric.\n## Prerequisites\nTo get started with this tutorial, check the following prerequisites:\n1. You should have access to a [SQL analytics endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/data-warehousing#sql-analytics-endpoint-of-the-lakehouse) or [Warehouse](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/data-warehousing#fabric-data-warehouse) within a [Premium capacity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/enterprise/service-premium-what-is) workspace with contributor or higher permissions.\n2. Choose your querying tool.\n2.1. Use the [SQL query editor in the Microsoft Fabric portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/sql-query-editor).\n2.2. Use the [Visual query editor in the Microsoft Fabric portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/visual-query-editor).\n3. Alternatively, you can use any of these tools to connect to your [SQL analytics endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/data-warehousing#sql-analytics-endpoint-of-the-lakehouse) or [Warehouse](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/data-warehousing#fabric-data-warehouse) via a T-SQL connection string. For more information, see [Connectivity](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/connectivity).\n3.1. [Download SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/ssms/download-sql-server-management-studio-ssms).\n3.2. Download and install both [Visual Studio Code and the MSSQL extension](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/tools/visual-studio-code/mssql-extensions?view=fabric&preserve-view=true).\nNote\nReview the [T-SQL surface area in Fabric Data Warehouse](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/tsql-surface-area) for SQL analytics endpoint or Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/query-warehouse"},{"title":"Connect to Fabric Data Warehouse","content":"# Connect to Fabric Data Warehouse\n## Connect using Power BI\nA Warehouse or Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint is a fully supported and native data source within Power BI, and there's no need to use the SQL Connection string. The **Data** pane exposes all of the warehouses you have access to directly. This allows you to easily find your warehouses by workspace, and:\n1. Select the Warehouse.\n2. Choose entities.\n3. Load Data - choose a data connectivity mode: [import or DirectQuery](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/connect-data/desktop-directquery-about).\nFor more information, see [Create reports on data warehousing in Microsoft Fabric](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/create-reports).\n## Connect using OLE DB\nWe support connectivity to the Warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint using OLE DB. Make sure you're running the [latest ODBC Driver for SQL Server](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/odbc/download-odbc-driver-for-sql-server). Use Microsoft Entra ID authentication. Great instinct — and the punchline is that the list is cheaper than it looks, because of a framing decision: **don't build Azure-branded adapters, build engine-generic ones** (which is also what ADR 0010/0013 anti-lock-in demands). Two generic adapters plus one small extension cover almost everything you named:

**1. A generic PostgreSQL adapter — the best ROI on the list.** GX Core supports Postgres natively via SQLAlchemy, so this reuses the exact shape of the Snowflake path: a `ConnectionAdapter` + a thin `CheckRunner` on the shared `gx_runner`, a registry entry, and a connection-spec for the add-connection drawer. One adapter then covers:
- **Azure Database for PostgreSQL** (Flexible Server)
- **Azure HorizonDB** — I checked the current docs: it's fully PostgreSQL-compatible with standard connection strings, drivers, and `sslmode=require`, so it works through a generic PG adapter with zero HorizonDB-specific code. Caveat: it's still **Preview**, so we'd support it as "it's Postgres" rather than advertise a named integration until GA.
- For free: AWS RDS, GCP Cloud SQL, self-hosted PG — a genuinely cloud-neutral datasource, which matters for the BYOL/marketplace story (ADR 0013).
- Bonus: we can dogfood it against our own app DB locally, so integration tests need no new harness infra.

**2. A generic MSSQL/T-SQL adapter — this is how you get Fabric.** To answer your question directly: **yes, Fabric is a datasource** — its Warehouse, Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint, and Fabric SQL database all expose a standard SQL Server TDS endpoint (port 1433, ODBC 18+/pyodbc, GX supports mssql via SQLAlchemy). One mssql adapter covers Fabric Warehouse + Lakehouse endpoints, **Azure SQL Database**, and Synapse dedicated pools. The one real design cost: Fabric endpoints want **Entra ID auth** (user or service principal; SQL auth isn't supported on some Fabric items), so the adapter needs a client-credentials token flow — but that's a solved pattern for us (same Key-Vault-held secret model, and we already do Entra service-principal auth for ADF).

**3. OneLake files — a small extension, not a new adapter.** OneLake speaks the ADLS Gen2 DFS API (`onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com`), so our existing ADLS flat-file adapter likely reaches Fabric lake files with just an endpoint override + Entra auth. Worth a spike before promising it.

**4. Cosmos DB — the odd one out; I'd defer it.** It has no SQL dialect SQLAlchemy/GX can drive, and GX is tabular. The honest options are (a) read containers into a DataFrame via the Cosmos SDK (the UC-runner shape) — workable for small containers but RU-cost and scale problems make it a bad default, or (b) **check it via its Fabric mirror** — Cosmos (and HorizonDB, incidentally) mirror into OneLake, where the mssql adapter reads it through the SQL analytics endpoint. Option (b) means Cosmos coverage falls out of #2 for anyone on Fabric, and a native adapter can wait for real demand.

So my recommendation, as a post-v1 theme: **PG adapter first** (smallest, most-requested DQ target in the market, cloud-neutral), **then mssql/Fabric**, **then the OneLake spike**, with Cosmos explicitly deferred-via-mirror. It slots cleanly alongside the current recommended opening (Theme-1 `schema_drift`/`anomaly`) rather than competing with it — different layer of the stack, and the seams mean neither blocks the other.

Want me to write this up as a new theme in `context/post-v1-roadmap.md` (with the four items + the HorizonDB-preview and Entra-auth caveats) and file the corresponding issues?

The app's DB is a distinct **`dataq`** database + least-priv **`dataq_app`** role on the **shared `dataq-pg-wus3-*`** server (1-of-each free/trial cap → env + Postgres shared with the harness, neutral-named `purpose=dataq-shared`; harness Postgres backed-up→recreated→restored). Azure AD **SSO app registrations** (API + SPA) created in TF + wired; migrate job ran `alembic upgrade head`; API healthy (401 = auth-enforced), SPA + deep-links 200, GitHub OIDC secrets/vars + `production` env set. Fixed **#393** (opencensus AzureLogHandler `lock=None` on Py3.13) en route. **GHCR package→repo connect done** (Actions-access grant → CI's `GITHUB_TOKEN` can push) and the **Deploy workflow validated end-to-end** (#403 fixed the migrate-command + frontend-pnpm bugs #401/#402; build→push→`alembic upgrade head`→ACA roll + SWA deploy all green on `v6`). **Post-deploy hardening (2026-06-28):** two production bugs surfaced and fixed — **#405** (Celery beat crashed on startup: the embedded `worker -B` beat re-nulled `self.lock` inside the opencensus `AzureLogHandler.createLock` fork on Python 3.13, silently killing ALL periodic tasks — orchestration polling, scheduled-suite dispatch, gap recovery, and sample-failure purge; fixed by making `createLock` idempotent in `backend/app/core/logging.py` + a network-free regression test; **#407** merged) and **#406** (deployed app couldn't read Key Vault: `AzureKeyVaultStore` called `DefaultAzureCredential()` with no args but the api+worker container runs a USER-assigned managed identity and `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` was unset — blocked connection tests, suite runs, AND orchestration polling; fixed by adding `AZURE_CLIENT_ID = azurerm_user_assigned_identity.app.client_id` to `local.app_env` in `deploy/terraform/azure/containerapps.tf`; **#408** merged). Backend image `:v7` built+pushed from main (with #405+#406); api+worker rolled to v7; App Insights re-enabled on the worker (the #405 mitigation of temporarily dropping `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` on the worker is reverted) — landed as **#409** (`image_tag` default v4→v7). **Orchestration polling is now live end-to-end** — beat starts clean (zero NoneType crashes) with App Insights on, api healthy (401, auth-enforced), ADF+Airflow connections polling via the 10-min beat fallback, Key Vault secrets read successfully. **Post-deploy feature batch (2026-06-29, all merged; prod image `:v7`→`:v10`):** Slack + email alert publishers behind the `ResultPublisher` seam (#413, `:v8`), column-aware failing-sample redaction (#417) + the #383/#384/#395/#423 hardening batch (`:v9`, bump #414), URL-encode DB password (#421/#395), always-alert operationally-failed runs (#419), alerting upsert race fix (#420/#384), per-run check outcome in the runs table (#425/#423), mypy gate over `backend/tests` (#418), and — **pulling ADR 0012 post-v1 Theme A forward — freshness & volume monitor-kinds end-to-end** (run engine #426 + authoring path & check-editor UI #437, `:v10`, bump #438). Three post-v1 design docs landed (#422/#430/#436) and are consolidated in **[context/post-v1-roadmap.md](context/post-v1-roadmap.md)** (the single post-v1 home + week-wise-task-generator input). **W7 in-repo work now DONE:** the **FastMCP 8-tool server** at `/mcp` (Azure-AD `JWTVerifier`-validated, fail-closed; ADR 0008, #460); the **hardening/docs pass** — prod-docs gate (#464), Swagger completeness + error-shape audit (#465), deployment guide + complete env-var reference (#468); **consistency hardening** — trigger-dedup index (#456, closes #308) + stuck-run reaper (#458, closes #309); the **visual-fidelity pass** (#459); and the W1–6 deferred + not-started triages (#463/#467, closing #169/#170). **W7 close-out batch (2026-07-01/02, all merged):** OTel **request/task spans** to App Insights (#525 — vendor-neutral core `backend/app/core/tracing.py` + Azure exporter-only, module-scope FastAPI + producer/consumer Celery instrumentation, secret/PII-safe span attributes, `dataq.request_id` span↔log join; opencensus→OTel log migration → #524) · **vault lazy-import test coverage** (#523, `secrets.py` 100%) · **#17 MCP polish** (#522 — this file's `.mcp.json` appendix + CONTRIBUTING rule 39 (numbered 38 pre-#547)) · **Playwright E2E expansion** (#526 schedules/triggers/notifications panels + #527 run-detail sample/dashboard/check-editor variants/admin — 25 specs green in CI) · **opt-in live-smoke lane** (#531 — `frontend/e2e-live/` gated on `E2E_LIVE_BASE_URL` with captured-OIDC session + `e2e_smoke.py` `DATAQ_BEARER` mode + runbook checklist; never in CI) · **user-docs enrichment** (#528 — notifications/scheduling/best-practices/feature-matrix pages; #532 filed) · **MCP tool-expansion candidates** (#530 — post-v1 Theme 13 + issue #529). **LIVE SMOKE RUN + #492 DONE (2026-07-02, via the #531 lane):** browser lane 3/3 · `e2e_smoke.py` bearer-mode vs prod · **Flows A/B/C verified green** (Snowflake ×3 / UC / flat-file) · **#525 spans confirmed in App Insights** · **MCP 4-query protocol smoke passed** vs live `/mcp` · **#492 closed** — Action Group + `PipelineFailedRuns` metric alert on the harness factory; a deliberate `pl_dataq_smoke_fail` failure was visible in DataQ **4m14s** after fire (Common-Alert-Schema → `AlertPing` → immediate-poll ingest, #534). The **api moved to internal ingress** (reached only via the frontend nginx proxy `/api` + `/mcp` + `/healthz`); the SWA (`dataq-app-web`) is **destroyed**. Landed as **#509** (cutover) → **#510** (lifecycle guards — `ignore_changes` on container images so applies never roll prod back to `var.image_tag`, + on the api `identifier_uris` so applies never strip the token audience) → **#511** (three ACA gotchas: nginx must proxy **HTTP/1.1** or ACA ingress 426s; api ingress **HTTP + `allow_insecure_connections`**; **orphaned SWA-EasyAuth** on the api disabled via `az containerapp auth update --enabled false` — it 401'd every request post-SWA-destroy; DataQ does its own `fastapi-azure-auth` validation). Prod frontend image `:v2`; URL `https://dataq-app-frontend.purplefield-f7322a1b.westus2.azurecontainerapps.io`. Follow-up **#512** (multi-arch frontend QEMU build was impractically slow/flaky — 45-min stall → cancel) **fixed in #518**: pin the frontend Dockerfile `build` stage to `--platform=$BUILDPLATFORM` so the arch-neutral Vite build runs natively once and only the per-arch nginx `serve` stage differs — frontend publish dropped from a 45-min stall to **~1min**, and a native-arm64 `:latest` multi-arch is published reliably again. # Audit — PR #576 (`docs/split-progress-ledger` @ e94fbe89)

## 1. Scope vs description — PASS

`git diff main...HEAD --stat`:

Matches the description with one addition not called out in the prompt: `README.md:7` also got its v1-ledger pointer repointed ("The completed v1 ledger is archived at docs/progress-v1.md; live post-v1 progress at docs/progress.md"). This is consistent with the stated intent and not a problem — just noting it's outside the explicitly-listed file set. `CLAUDE.md`'s diff hunk is confined to §12 (line 277) and §13 (lines 284, 295); `context/post-v1-roadmap.md`'s diff is confined to the intro (lines 7–10) and the G-h row (line 66), exactly as described.

## 2. Link integrity — PASS

Every relative link in the new `docs/progress.md` resolves from `docs/`: `progress-v1.md`, `retro-v1.md`, `adr/0026-auth-api-keys-and-principal-seam.md`, `../context/post-v1-roadmap.md` — all exist. Cross-checked the repo-root-relative links added in `CLAUDE.md` (`docs/progress.md`, `docs/progress-v1.md`), `context/README.md` and `context/post-v1-roadmap.md` (`../docs/progress-v1.md`, `../docs/progress.md`), and `docs/retro-v1.md` (`progress-v1.md`) — all resolve. Also ran `mkdocs build --strict` locally — clean build, zero warnings/errors (the tool's own `validation:` block is set to `ignore` for omitted/absolute/unrecognized links, but strict mode still would have failed on a truly broken nav/exclude entry, and it didn't).

## 3. Stale `progress.md` references — CONDITIONAL (repo-wide grep, excluding `.git`/`node_modules`/`site`)

**Correctly pointing at the live tracker (fine, no action):**

- `CLAUDE.md:277,284,304,306` — §12/§13 live-tracker pointers, all correct post-split.

- `docs/progress.md`, `docs/progress-v1.md` internal self/companion links — correct.

**🟡 Stale — semantically mean the frozen v1 ledger but still say `progress.md` (should now say `progress-v1.md`):**

Not touched by this PR even though §9 wasn't explicitly excluded from scope. |

## 4. Factual accuracy of new `docs/progress.md` — PASS

- **53 open issues, all `Backlog (post-v1 / testing)`** — verified via `gh issue list --state open --limit 100 --json number,milestone`: exactly 53 open issues returned, every one on that milestone. Matches `docs/progress.md:27`.
- **Carried-over issue numbers all open** — `#466, #563, #568, #571, #573, #194, #195, #197, #199, #204, #327, #349, #351, #372, #524, #529, #532, #505, #461` — all 19 present in the open-issue list above. Confirmed open.
- **Coverage numbers** — `docs/progress.md:29` claims "98.4% / 1,289 tests" backend and "~88% / 337 tests" frontend "at the tag." `docs/retro-v1.md:23-24` and the `v1.0.0` GitHub release notes (`gh release view v1.0.0`) both independently state "1,289 backend tests, 98.4% line coverage" and "337 frontend tests, ~88% all-src line coverage" — exact match across all three sources.
- **"187/189"** — matches `docs/progress-v1.md`'s Aggregate table exactly: `TOTAL | 187 | 0 | 2 | 189`.
- **#177 closed with the tag** — `gh issue view 177` confirms `closedAt: 2026-07-04T04:29:01Z`, consistent with the archive banner's "closed with the `v1.0.0` tag later that same day" note (54→53).

## 5. Archive banner consistency (`docs/progress-v1.md`) — PASS

Lines 1–15: frozen at `v1.0.0` (2026-07-04) ✓, points to `progress.md` and `retro-v1.md` ✓ (both resolve), point-in-time 54→53 note is factually correct per #177's closedAt timestamp ✓. "How to update this file" (lines 562–576) carries the historical marker: "**Historical** — this archive is frozen; the process below now applies to the live [progress.md](progress.md)." ✓

## 6. mkdocs — PASS

`progress-v1.md` is present in `exclude_docs` (alongside `progress.md`, added this PR — `mkdocs.yml:80`). `nav:` (lines 57-71) references neither `progress.md` nor `progress-v1.md`. Confirmed with a local strict build (clean, zero warnings).

## 7. CLAUDE.md §13 "Open follow-ups" sentence — PASS

Line 304's "Open follow-ups (full register in `docs/progress.md`...)" still makes sense: the new `docs/progress.md`'s "Carried over from v1" section (Long-standing follow-ups table, lines 53-69) contains every issue number cited in that §13 sentence (#327, #372, #349, #351, #197, #199, #204, #194, #195), so the register genuinely lives at the linked location now.

## Cross-reference summary

- ADR count: N/A to this PR (no ADR files added/removed).
- Links checked in new/edited files: ~14 relative links across `docs/progress.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, `context/README.md`, `context/post-v1-roadmap.md`, `docs/retro-v1.md` — 0 broken.
- `progress.md`/`progress-v1.md` mentions repo-wide (excl. `.git`/`node_modules`/`site`): ~30 total; 9 flagged as stale-but-non-hyperlinked (ADR footers + CLAUDE.md §9), 2 borderline/ambiguous, rest correct.

## Verdict

**Conditional — 1 concern (9 stale-but-non-broken ADR/CLAUDE.md §9 references still say `docs/progress.md` when they mean the now-archived `docs/progress-v1.md`).** Nothing here breaks a link or misstates a fact checked in items 4–7; the repo is internally consistent and the mkdocs strict build is clean. Recommend a small follow-up PR (or a fixup on this branch) to repoint the 6 ADR files' "Related"/footer notes (`0005`, `0010`, `0011`, `0012`, `0021`×2, `0022`×2) and `CLAUDE.md:229` from `docs/progress.md` to `docs/progress-v1.md` before it's forgotten — these are exactly the kind of "reads fine today, misleads in 3 months" drift the archive split was meant to prevent. This is a concrete, actionable item; recommend filing/fixing via `/gh-issue-from-finding` per working-agreement #3 if not folded into this same PR.

> DEVELOPER

If you could add one unrequested, industry-leading feature, what would it be?

> AGENT

**Agentic root-cause analysis** — when a check fails, DataQ doesn't just alert you, it *investigates* and hands you a diagnosis.

Here's why that one, and not the obvious candidates. Auto-suggested checks and anomaly baselines (G-a) are the biggest gap, but they're catch-up — Anomalo and Monte Carlo already pitch automatic coverage; building them makes DataQ competitive, not leading. The thing nobody in the category actually ships is closing the loop *after* detection: every DQ product today ends at "row count dropped 40% 🔴" and a human spends the next two hours figuring out why.

DataQ is unusually well-positioned to own that moment, because the expensive raw material is already in the schema:

- **`pipeline_runs` ↔ `runs` correlation** — the `triggered_by` link means DataQ already knows *which ADF/Airflow run produced the data that just failed*, its timing, and whether the pipeline itself erred or ran long. Cron-only checkers (Soda, Elementary in most deployments) structurally can't do this.
- **`metric_value` as a SQL-aggregatable scalar** (ADR 0012) — trend context for "is this sudden or a slow drift" is a query, not a new pipeline.
- **Redacted failing samples + the column profiler** — the evidence for "which segment broke" is one profiling call away.
- **The MCP server** — the agent plumbing exists; today it points outward (Claude asks DataQ questions). This feature points it inward.

The v1 slice: on a `fail`/`critical` result, a Celery task assembles the dossier — upstream pipeline run (status, duration vs. its own history, delay), the check's `metric_value` trend, a profile-diff of the failing batch vs. the last passing one, sibling checks on the same table — and an LLM turns it into a three-sentence narrative with a confidence-ranked cause: *"Orders freshness failed because `pl_ingest_orders` ran 47 min late; the volume drop is confined to `region = EMEA`, consistent with the upstream API timeout in the pipeline's error output. Downstream suites X and Y consume this table."* That narrative rides the existing `ResultPublisher` seam straight into the Teams/Slack alert — the alert people currently get, but with the two hours of triage pre-done.

It also compounds with everything already planned: it *is* the incident half of gap G-d, it gets sharper as Theme-1's anomaly baselines land, and it turns the MCP server from "nice integration" into the product's core loop. That's the leap from "tells you something broke" to "tells you what happened" — and that's a category-defining claim, not a feature-parity one.

> DEVELOPER

but this will be only possible if user add an LLM connection. Right?

> AGENT

Yes for the narrative, no for most of the value — and that split is exactly how I'd design it.

The two layers:

**The dossier is deterministic — no LLM anywhere.** Correlating the failed run to its upstream pipeline run, comparing the pipeline's duration/delay to its own history, pulling the `metric_value` trend, diffing the failing batch's profile against the last passing one, listing sibling checks and downstream suites — that's all SQL and existing profiler calls. Shipped as a structured "evidence card" on the alert (*pipeline late by 47 min · metric 3.2σ below its 30-day mean · drop concentrated in `region = EMEA`*), it's already most of the two hours of triage, with zero new dependencies. Honestly, this layer alone would be a strong feature.

**The narrative + ranked hypothesis is where the LLM comes in** — and yes, that requires the user to configure one. Three things make that dependency palatable:

1. **It's BYO and optional, behind a seam.** Same pattern as everything else in DataQ (ADR 0010/0011): a generic `LLMProvider` with the user's own endpoint/key — Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, or any OpenAI-compatible/local endpoint — stored in Key Vault like any connection secret. No LLM configured → you get the evidence card; LLM configured → you get the narrative on top. Fail-open to the deterministic layer, never a hard dependency. And Theme 2's LLM-assisted check authoring needs this exact seam anyway, so it's one connection type serving two roadmap features.
2. **The MCP server is the zero-config escape hatch.** DataQ already speaks MCP — so a user's *existing* Claude/Copilot can be the reasoning engine, with DataQ just serving the evidence through tools. "Ask your assistant *why did this run fail?* and it investigates via `/mcp`" gives you interactive RCA without DataQ ever holding an LLM key. The push-narrative-into-the-alert version is the premium ergonomics; the MCP version is the same capability for free.
3. **The privacy story is already built.** Whatever goes to the model passes through the existing column-aware redaction (#417) — the LLM sees the redacted samples and aggregates, same as a non-admin user would. That's usually the first objection enterprises raise, and DataQ's answer predates the feature.

So the honest framing: the LLM connection buys the last 20% (prose, causal ranking, cross-signal reasoning), the schema you already have buys the first 80%. Which is also the right shipping order — evidence card first, narrative as the follow-up once the `LLMProvider` seam lands.

> DEVELOPER

Great. Let's add it to the road map

> AGENT

Adding it. Let me look at where it fits in the roadmap's theme structure (it touches Theme 2's LLM work, Theme 5 alerting, and gap G-d's incident workflow).

[PR #577](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/577) is open with the design capture, audited clean, CI running — I'll merge on green.

What landed in the roadmap:

- **Theme 2 gets an "Agentic root-cause analysis" subsection** — placed there because that's where the `LLMProvider` seam already lives, so the authoring work and this feature explicitly share one seam. The capture records the full shape from our discussion: layer 1 (deterministic evidence card — pipeline correlation, `metric_value` trend, profile-diff, blast radius — on the `ResultPublisher` seam, **build first**, zero new dependencies), layer 2 (optional BYO-credential LLM narrative, fail-open to layer 1, column-aware-redacted context), and the zero-config MCP path where the user's own assistant does the investigating.
- **Gap G-d cross-referenced** — the row now notes its incident-*narrative* half is design-captured here, while lineage/incident-objects still need their own design doc (unchanged).
- **No issues filed yet**, per the doc's convention — with an explicit note that the two layers should file as *separate* issues when picked up, since layer 1 can ship alone.

The docs-consistency-guard verified every technical claim in the capture against the repo (the `triggered_by` unique index and `PipelineRun` model, `metric_value` as `Numeric`, ADR 0011/0012, #417 being the column-aware redaction PR) — so the design text is grounded, not aspirational.

> DEVELOPER

Any other new feature, optimization or update you can suggest based on our privacy focused, vendor neutral, and other themes.

> AGENT

Yes — a handful, and I'll hold myself to the same bar as the RCA one: each has to ride an existing seam, not duplicate something already themed, and be defensible as *leading* rather than parity. Grouped by your axes:

**Privacy-focused**

1. **PII auto-classification with tag-driven redaction + "PII drift" alerts.** Today #417's redaction is column-name-heuristic. Upgrade: the profiler (which already visits every column) runs lightweight PII detectors (regex/format heuristics — no LLM needed), persists a per-column classification tag, and the redaction layer reads *tags* instead of guessing from names. The leading part: once columns carry classifications, a **`pii_drift` monitor kind** falls out of the ADR 0012 seam almost free — "a column that looks like email addresses just appeared in a table not marked as containing PII" is an alert none of the mainstream DQ tools fire, and it's the incident privacy teams actually fear. Compounds with Theme 4 (compliance) and Theme 1 (`schema_drift`).

2. **Zero-sample "privacy mode."** A deployment-level switch where failing-row samples are never persisted at all — only aggregates, `metric_value`, and unexpected-counts. The retention sweep already PII-minimises after the fact; this is the stricter promise ("row values never leave your warehouse") that HIPAA-tier and EU deployments ask about first. Cheap to build (it's mostly a write-path gate), and it converts the existing redaction stack from a feature into a tiered privacy posture: full → column-aware redacted → zero-sample.

**Vendor-neutral**

3. **Generic OTLP observability endpoint.** This is the one deferred seam from ADR 0010 that's still half-open: #525 made tracing OTel-native in core, but the exporter is Azure-only, and #524 (logs) is heading the same way. Adding a plain `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` config path makes App Insights just one backend — Grafana/Tempo, Datadog, Jaeger, anything OTLP works. It's the observability twin of the `DATAQ_AUTH_*` generic-OIDC cutover you already did for auth, and it matters for the BYOL/marketplace story (ADR 0013): a customer on AWS shouldn't need App Insights to see traces.

4. **Generic signed-webhook `ResultPublisher`.** Teams/Slack/email exist; one HMAC-signed outbound webhook publisher (mirroring the Airflow *ingest* signing pattern you already have) makes the alerting side vendor-neutral in a single impl — PagerDuty, Opsgenie, ntfy, home-grown routers, all without bespoke publishers. Payload goes through the same redaction rules. Highest leverage-per-line-of-code on this list.

5. **S3-compatible endpoint override** — one config field on the existing S3 adapter (`endpoint_url`) unlocks MinIO, Cloudflare R2, and on-prem object stores. Same shape as the OneLake spike from the Theme-8 batch; near-zero cost.

**Developer-workflow (the biggest strategic one)**

6. **Checks-as-code: `dataq.yaml` + a CI gate.** The export/import format, the API, and (once ADR 0026's PATs land) the auth already exist — formalizing them into a versioned declarative suite format plus a CLI/GitHub-Action (`dataq validate` in a data-pipeline repo's CI, `dataq apply` to sync, drift detection between repo and workspace) is how data-platform teams actually want to manage checks. Soda and GX Cloud lead with this workflow; DataQ's angle is that its format round-trips with a full UI *and* the suite-scoped authz model — most checks-as-code tools have no real UI, most UI tools have no real GitOps. It also gives ADR 0026 its killer use case, which strengthens the argument for scheduling PATs early.

If I had to rank: **#6 and #1 are roadmap-theme material** (market-positioning weight, like the RCA capture), **#3 and #4 are the best effort-to-value ratio** and could each be a single Backlog issue today, **#2 and #5 are cheap riders** to note wherever their neighbors land.

316	## Theme 13 — MCP tool expansion (candidate endpoints)
317	
318	The v1 MCP server exposes 8 curated tools (ADR [0008](../docs/adr/0008-mcp-server.md));
319	the REST surface has ~52 more endpoints. Candidates below, tiered by risk — every new
320	tool stays a thin service-layer wrapper with `require_permission` authz + sample
321	redaction, exactly like the existing 8 (`backend/app/mcp/server.py`). Cross-cutting
322	dependencies: **#488** (workspace-admin visibility in MCP tools) and **#461 / ADR 0026**
323	(DataQ-issued API keys, which unblock headless MCP clients).
324	
325	**Tier 1 — high-value safe reads:**
326	
327	| Candidate tool | Wraps | NL query it serves |
328	|---|---|---|
329	| `list_checks` / `get_check` | `GET /suites/{id}/checks[/{id}]` | "what checks does the orders suite have?" |
330	| `get_check_history` | `GET .../checks/{id}/history` | "how has null-rate trended this week?" |
331	| `list_runs` | `GET /runs` (filterable) | "show me yesterday's failed runs" |
332	| `get_run_results` | `GET /runs/{id}` (redacted) | "why did run X fail?" |
333	| `list_connections` | `GET /connections` — names/types/health **only, never config or secrets** | "which connections are unhealthy?" |
334	| `list_schedules` | `GET /schedules` | "when does the orders suite run?" |
335	| `list_trigger_bindings` | `GET /trigger-bindings` | "what triggers the gold suite?" |
336	| `get_notification_config` | `GET /suites/{id}/notifications` | "who gets alerted for this suite?" |
337	| `get_suite_performance` | `GET /dashboard/summary` (per-suite slice) | "which suite is worst this month?" |
338	| `export_suite` | `GET /suites/{id}/export` | "export the orders suite" |
339	
340	**Tier 2 — mutating, edit-permission-gated:**
341	
342	| Candidate tool | Wraps | Note |
343	|---|---|---|
344	| `dryrun_check` | `POST /suites/{id}/checks/dryrun` | the LLM author-preview loop — pairs with `create_check` |
345	| `update_check` / `delete_check` | `PATCH`/`DELETE` check | delete needs confirm-style ergonomics |
346	| `snooze_check` / `unsnooze_check` | check snooze endpoints | "snooze this alert for 24h" |
347	| `cancel_run` | `POST /runs/{id}/cancel` | |
348	| `create_schedule` / `delete_schedule` | schedules CRUD | "run this suite daily at 9am IST" |
349	| `create_trigger_binding` | `POST /trigger-bindings` | "run this suite when the orders DAG succeeds" |
350	| `import_suite` | `POST /suites/import` | |
351	| `suggest_column_policy` | `POST /suites/{id}/column-policy/suggest` | redaction-policy assistant |
352	| `test_connection` | `POST /connections/{id}/test` | action but non-destructive |
353	
354	**Excluded (deliberate):** connection create/update/reauth (**credentials transiting an
355	LLM — hard no**); the orchestration webhooks (M2M surface); admin endpoints (workspace-
356	admin scoping pending #488); share mutations (permission escalation through a
357	conversational interface); `_probe` (demo-only); `/me` + `/users/search` (low value).
358	
359	---

All design-captured, no issues filed yet.\n\n### Checks-as-code: `dataq.yaml` + a CI gate\n\nFormalize the existing export/import format into a **versioned declarative suite format** plus a\nCLI / GitHub Action: `dataq validate` in a data-pipeline repo's CI, `dataq apply` to sync,\n**drift detection** between repo and workspace. The market leaders (Soda, GX Cloud) lead with\nthis workflow; DataQ's angle is that the format **round-trips with a full UI and the\nsuite-scoped authz model** — checks-as-code tools mostly have no real UI, UI tools no real\nGitOps. Hard dependency: **ADR 0026 / #461** (PATs) — this is its killer use case, and the\nargument for scheduling PATs early in the cycle.\n\n### Incident / ITSM — tier 2, bidirectional\n\nTier 1 (create-only PagerDuty / Opsgenie / ServiceNow / Jira via the generic signed-webhook\npublisher + payload templates) lives in **Theme 5** and needs zero vendor code. Tier 2 is the\nITSM-grade half: DataQ incident objects (the G-d design) sync *both ways* — ack/resolve in\nPagerDuty/ServiceNow reflects in DataQ, Jira issue links attach to results — and the **Theme 2\nagentic-RCA evidence card is the incident payload**, so the ticket arrives with the diagnosis\npre-attached. Per-vendor impls behind one `IncidentProvider`-shaped seam, only after tier 1\nproves demand.\n\n### Test-management publishing (TestRail, Xray, Zephyr)\n\nDQ artifacts map cleanly: suites → test plans, checks → cases, runs → test runs with results.\nA result-*exporter* seam (a `ResultPublisher` sibling — per-run push, not per-alert) publishes\nrun outcomes into the test-management tool of record; pairs with Theme 9's PDF export (#345)\nas the \"reporting into someone else's system of record\" family.\n\n### Data-governance catalogs (+ OpenLineage)\n\nTwo directions, one seam:\n\n- **Pull** — consume the catalog's glossary/PII classifications as an authoritative\n  classification source (feeds Theme 4's privacy pack + #433, ranked above profiler\n  heuristics), and **pull lineage** to power the RCA blast-radius (Theme 2) and gap G-d\n  instead of building a lineage graph ourselves.\n- **Push** — publish DQ results as **quality facets/assertions on catalog entities**, so data\n  consumers see check status where they shop for data. [PR #578](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/578) is up and audited — CI is rerunning after a small fixup; I'll merge on green. Here's what landed, plus direct answers to your two questions:

**Yes, the vendor-neutral alerting approach covers most of the integration ask** — that's the design the roadmap now records in two tiers:
- **Tier 1 (Theme 5, zero vendor code):** the generic HMAC-signed webhook `ResultPublisher` plus a per-destination payload-template layer reaches **PagerDuty (Events API v2), Opsgenie, ServiceNow (inbound REST), and Jira (Automation inbound webhooks)** — all four have generic inbound receivers, so DataQ never needs to know who's on the other end. The already-filed #389 rename is the prerequisite.
- **Tier 2 (new Theme 14, per-vendor, only if demand proves out):** true ITSM-grade *bidirectional* sync — ack/resolve in PagerDuty/ServiceNow reflecting back into DataQ, Jira issue links on results — behind one `IncidentProvider`-shaped seam, with the agentic-RCA evidence card as the incident payload (the ticket arrives with the diagnosis attached). **TestRail** is deliberately separate: it's not alerting but result *export* (suites→test plans, runs→test runs), captured as a per-run exporter seam.

**And yes, data governance is absolutely an angle — arguably the best synergy on the board.** Captured in Theme 14 as two directions through one seam: **pull** (consume the catalog's PII/glossary classifications — which feeds straight into the Theme-4 privacy pack — and pull *lineage* to power RCA blast-radius and gap G-d, instead of building a lineage graph ourselves) and **push** (publish DQ results as quality assertions on catalog entities, so data consumers see check status where they shop for data). The open-standards-first slice is **OpenLineage emission** from runs — one neutral event stream that Marquez, DataHub, Purview, and Atlan all consume — with DataHub/OpenMetadata as open-source reference impls and Purview covering the Azure story.

**Also in the batch:** the Theme-4 privacy pack (PII auto-detection, `pii_drift` monitor kind, zero-sample privacy mode), the S3-compatible endpoint row in Theme 8, checks-as-code as Theme 14's opening capture (explicitly naming ADR 0026/PATs as its hard dependency — strengthens the case for scheduling PATs early), and the generic-OTLP observability row. The audit also caught that Backlog issues **#524 and #505 had never been mapped to any theme** — a violation of the roadmap's own mirroring invariant — so Theme 14's portability table now fixes that, and the theme count in progress.md went 13 → 14.

> DEVELOPER

In the data sources part, what do you think we are missing? The major ones, the no brainer ones.

> AGENT

Looking at the market with the Theme-8 batch already in (PG, MSSQL/Fabric, OneLake, S3-compatible), the gaps sort cleanly into "complete the cloud triads" and "one federation multiplier":

**The two glaring warehouse gaps:**

1. **BigQuery** — the biggest single omission on the board. Snowflake/Databricks/BigQuery is the modern warehouse top-three, and DataQ covers two of them. GX supports it via `sqlalchemy-bigquery`, so it's the same shape as the Snowflake path: dialect + connection-spec + service-account-key auth in the SecretStore. Without it, every GCP-side prospect is a non-starter.
2. **Amazon Redshift** — the AWS warehouse. We already do S3, and AWS shops almost always pair the two; having the file half but not the warehouse half of the AWS stack is an odd gap. Also cheap: Redshift is Postgres-dialect-adjacent (`sqlalchemy-redshift`), so it lands as a near-sibling of the generic PG adapter.

**The flat-file completion:**

3. **Google Cloud Storage** — we do ADLS Gen2 and S3; GCS completes the object-store trio, and the `FlatFileCheckRunner` already does the hard part (pandas + batch resolution). It's mostly a third `ConnectionAdapter` + `gcsfs`. Together with #1 and #2, this gives the clean marketing sentence the BYOL story (ADR 0013) wants: **warehouse + object store covered on all three clouds.**

**The OLTP sibling:**

4. **MySQL/MariaDB** — the other half of the open-source OLTP world after Postgres. Once the generic-PG adapter proves the "engine-generic SQLAlchemy runner" pattern, MySQL is a dialect swap. Enormous installed base, near-zero marginal cost.

**The multiplier (my favorite of the bunch):**

5. **Trino — which also gets you Athena.** One SQLAlchemy dialect, and you inherit Trino's entire connector ecosystem: users point DataQ at their existing Trino/Starburst cluster and can check Hive, Iceberg, Cassandra, Mongo, Kafka-topics-as-tables — anything Trino federates — without us writing an adapter per store. And **Amazon Athena** rides the same family for the serverless-AWS crowd. This is the single cheapest answer to gap G-f's "4 datasources vs the 30–50 a category product ships": you don't ship 30 adapters, you ship the one that speaks to 30 things.

**Deliberately *not* no-brainers:** Oracle/Teradata/SAP HANA (real enterprise demand but heavy drivers/licensing — demand-driven, not default), MongoDB (same no-SQL-dialect logic as the Cosmos decided-against — same routing answer too, via Trino or a mirror), Kafka/streaming (not batch; that's the DQX v1.1 lane per ADR 0003), and Delta/Iceberg table formats on raw object storage — worth noting #286 already tracks Iceberg, and a `delta` flat-file format would slot next to the existing JSON row.

If you want, I'll add these to Theme 8 in the same style — BigQuery, Redshift, GCS, MySQL, Trino/Athena as `(no issue yet)` rows with a "cloud-triad completion" note, and a one-liner extending the decided-against section for the Oracle/Mongo/streaming boundary.

I have everything I need. All behavior confirmed empirically against sample payloads. Here are the findings.

---

## Review: PR #580 — `chore/progress-merge-hook` (`.claude/settings.json`)

**Scope reviewed:** the one changed file, `git diff main...HEAD` — a new `PostToolUse:Bash` merge-reminder hook plus the refreshed `docs/progress.md` / new `docs/progress-v1.md` hooks. I extracted each `command` with `jq`, ran it under `sh` against a battery of stdin payloads, and checked JSON validity, exit codes, and jq-missing behavior.

**What's correct (verified, no action needed):**
- All three emitted payloads parse as valid JSON with `hookSpecificOutput.hookEventName == "PostToolUse"` (checked via `jq -e`). No shell-quoting/JSON-escaping bugs in either changed `"command"` string — the `additionalContext` text contains no embedded `"`/`\` so nothing is mis-escaped.
- Progress-hook **case ordering is safe**: `*/docs/progress-v1.md` is matched by its own first case and routed to the archive message; `*/docs/progress.md` does not match a `progress-v1.md` path (confirmed empirically), so ordering is non-overlapping either way.
- Compound separators fire correctly: `&&`, `;`, `|`, and `||` (the `*"| gh pr merge"*` pattern does also catch `|| gh pr merge`, as predicted) all FIRE with valid JSON.
- Exit code is `0` on both the FIRES and silent paths, so the hook never breaks the underlying Bash tool call.
- The hook is live and working — it fired on my own test invocations this session.

No crash/correctness/data defects. The findings below are all in the hook's own matching precision (it is an advisory reminder, so impact is "reminder wrongly shown/omitted," never a broken command).

---

### Finding 1 (Important) — Merge on its own line / after a newline never fires (false negative that defeats the hook's purpose)

`.claude/settings.json:23` — pattern set `"gh pr merge"* | *"&& gh pr merge"* | *"; gh pr merge"* | *"| gh pr merge"*`.

A multi-line Bash command whose merge is on its own line is **silent**:
```
git push
gh pr merge 580 --squash
```
Verified: payload `"line1\ngh pr merge 580"` → silent. Same for a leading-whitespace command `"  gh pr merge 580"` and an env-prefixed `"FOO=1 gh pr merge 580"` — both silent. These are exactly the real merges the hook exists to catch, and multi-line/heredoc-style Bash tool commands are common, so the reminder will be missed on a meaningful fraction of genuine merges.

Root cause: `"gh pr merge"*` anchors at offset 0 only, and the separator patterns enumerate `&&`/`;`/`|` with exactly one surrounding space — newline, leading whitespace, and `&&`/`;` without the exact spacing are not covered.

**Concrete fix:** replace the glob `case` with a boundary regex on the command, which naturally handles newlines (grep is line-oriented, so a merge on any line matches `^`) and leading whitespace:
```sh
input=$(cat); cmd=$(printf '%s' "$input" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty');
if printf '%s' "$cmd" | grep -Eq '(^|[[:space:];&|])[[:space:]]*gh pr merge([[:space:]]|$)'; then printf '%s' '{...}'; fi
```
This catches own-line, leading-space, and tighter-spaced `&&gh pr merge` cases.

---

### Finding 2 (Minor) — Separator + phrase inside quoted commit/PR text still fires (the fixup's stated goal isn't fully met)

`.claude/settings.json:23`. The fixup commit c132df6d claims the hook "fires only on command-position matches … not on commit/PR text mentioning the phrase." That holds only when the quoted mention has no separator in front of it. When the quoted text itself contains a separator followed by the phrase, it **fires falsely** (all verified):
- `git commit -m "document how to run x && gh pr merge y"` → FIRES
- `git commit -m "steps: build; gh pr merge"` → FIRES
- `gh pr create --body "pipe it | gh pr merge"` → FIRES

This is an inherent limit of substring matching (it can't distinguish shell syntax from quoted string contents) and my suggested regex in Finding 1 does not fix it either. Impact is low — a spurious advisory reminder, no harm. Worth noting only so the PR description's "silent on mentions" claim isn't over-trusted; if you want to narrow it, gate the reminder to only when the Bash command *succeeded* (a real merge), though PostToolUse doesn't cleanly expose that here.

---

### Finding 3 (Nit) — `"gh pr merge"*` also matches `gh pr mergeXYZ`

`.claude/settings.json:23`. The prefix glob has no trailing word boundary, so `gh pr mergeZZZ` FIRES (verified). Harmless in practice — `gh pr merge` has no sibling subcommand with that prefix — but the boundary regex in Finding 1 (`([[:space:]]|$)` after `merge`) closes it for free.

---

### Not a defect (checked, reporting so it's not re-raised)

- **jq unguarded when missing:** with jq absent from PATH, the new Bash hook and both progress hooks exit `0`, produce empty stdout, and emit only `jq: command not found` on stderr — which PostToolUse ignores on a zero exit. So a missing jq does **not** break Bash tool calls. This matches the pre-existing sibling formatter hook at `.claude/settings.json:10`, which also calls `jq` unguarded while only guarding `black`/`ruff` with `command -v`. Consistent with existing convention; no change warranted unless you want to harden all three uniformly.

**Bottom line:** ship-able as an advisory hook. The one finding worth fixing before merge is **Finding 1** (own-line/newline merges silently miss the reminder), since it undercuts the hook's own goal on a common command shape; the regex swap fixes 1 and 3 together. Relevant file: `/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/.claude/settings.json` (lines 14 and 23).

Both fixups are in and CI is running on the two PRs (I'll merge on green). Now, the UI question — grouped by how users would feel them, and excluding what's already tracked (#345 PDF export, #283 version revert, #351 Test-Connection button, #466 browsing/pickers, #532 dry-run coverage, #424, Theme 12's dark mode):

**IA-level gaps (the two biggest):**

1. **A data-asset-centric view.** The whole UI is suite-centric, but users think table-centric: "is `orders` healthy?" today requires knowing which suites touch it. A dataset page — all checks, results, freshness state, and trend across every suite that targets that table/file pattern — is the single biggest navigation upgrade, and it's the natural UI anchor for the lineage/governance work (Theme 14) and the RCA blast-radius later. Category leaders (Monte Carlo, Atlan) are asset-first for exactly this reason.
2. **Global search / command palette (⌘K).** Suites, checks, connections, runs, admin — there's no way to jump anywhere by name. Cheap to build (the list APIs exist), disproportionate daily-use payoff, and it's the feature whose absence makes a product feel dated in 2026.

**Result-consumption gaps:**

3. **Per-check metric trend view.** ADR 0016/0012 deliberately store `metric_value` as an aggregatable scalar, and the dashboard uses it in aggregate — but there's no "this check over time" chart with the warn/fail/critical threshold bands drawn on it. That's the payoff view for the whole severity-derivation design, and it's one recharts component away.
4. **Run comparison (diff two runs).** "What changed between yesterday's pass and today's fail" — per-check status deltas, metric deltas, new/removed checks. Pairs naturally with the RCA evidence card; even standalone it kills a very common manual workflow.
5. **In-app notification center.** Alerts currently exist only as *outbound* Teams/Slack/email — a bell icon with the recent-alerts feed (read/ack state, deep link to the run) gives alerts a home for people who live in the app, and becomes the surface for incident state when Theme 14 tier-2 lands.

**Adoption/polish gaps:**

6. **First-run onboarding & empty states.** Connect → suite → check → run as a guided path. Matters little for the current solo deployment, but it's the first thing a marketplace/BYOL evaluator hits (ADR 0013), and empty-state quality is cheap to retrofit now versus embarrassing at listing time.
7. **Bulk operations** — multi-select checks for enable/disable/severity/snooze; anything beyond one-at-a-time editing on suites with 50+ checks.
8. **Accessibility pass (WCAG-level keyboard/contrast/screen-reader audit).** Never mentioned anywhere in the repo, and it converts from "nice" to "procurement checkbox" the moment a commercial buyer with compliance requirements shows up. Worth capturing so it's a decision, not an omission.

If you want these in the roadmap: Theme 3 already carries "UI/IA" in its title, so 1–2 and 6–8 slot there; 3–5 belong in Theme 9 (results depth) next to #345/#283. Say the word and I'll add them in the same design-captured/`(no issue yet)` style once the two open PRs land.

156	## Theme 3 — Admin, access model & UI/IA
157	
158	Full design: **[post-v1-admin-ui-notes.md](../docs/post-v1-admin-ui-notes.md)**. v1 ships suite-level sharing
159	+ a read-only workspace-admin view (#289). A full RBAC console is gold-plating for a single-tenant
160	trusted-team tool; the market leaders lead with checks→results→trends→alerts, not user-lifecycle.
161	
162	| # | Title |
163	|---|---|
164	| [#411](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/411) | Workspace-admin: workspace-wide view on Dashboard + Results (both are owned-or-shared scoped today) |
165	| [#412](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/412) | Admin page is read-only — allow workspace-admin write actions (manage shares / suites) |
166	| [#461](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/461) | **DataQ-issued API keys / service tokens** (REST + MCP) — see below |
167	
168	**DataQ-issued API keys / service tokens (#461, ADR [0026](../docs/adr/0026-auth-api-keys-and-principal-seam.md) proposed).** Auth today is Azure-AD-only (delegated/SSO) for both REST and `/mcp` — the deepest remaining vendor lock-in (the `get_current_user` seam has one real impl; `users.aad_object_id` is Azure-shaped) and it blocks BYOL-on-AWS/GCP (ADR 0013) and headless/programmatic access (a long-lived scoped key beats a ~60-min refreshing token for CI / always-on MCP clients). The fix is a **second authenticator behind the same `get_current_user` seam** so the **REST API and MCP accept it identically** — never MCP-only — which also finally *exercises* the seam (ADR 0010). Phase it: **user-scoped PATs first** (inherit the owner's per-suite grants → zero new authz; optional read-only down-scope), defer standalone **service-account principals** (they force generalizing `aad_object_id` → a generic principal with pluggable identity bindings + non-user suite sharing). Credential bar: hashed-at-rest + show-once + prefix + expiry + revocation + audit, in a new `api_keys` table (not the retrievable-secret SecretStore), with key lifecycle tied to the owner so it can't outlive a deactivated account.

Since you said "we need to think more on those lines," here's the thinking baked into it: the phasing is deliberately *ratchet-first* — wire `axe-core` into the Playwright lane and `vitest-axe` into component tests **before** any manual remediation, so CI stops new violations while the backlog is worked. The highest-user-impact single item is #2: severity in DataQ is communicated almost entirely by color (tags *and* the recharts series), which means roughly 8% of male users can't reliably read the product's core language — icons/shapes/text alongside a colorblind-safe palette fixes that. Then the keyboard/focus audit (the custom drawer/table/editor compositions are where antd's decent baseline breaks) and screen-reader semantics — where per-chart text alternatives do double duty as the data path for the #345 PDF export. The capture also plants the zero-cost habit now: stop hard-coding user-facing strings in new code, so i18n stays a config problem instead of a rewrite when a non-English prospect appears.

**Theme 9** gets the three result-consumption rows — the per-check `metric_value` trend chart with threshold bands (the view the ADR 0016 design was always pointing at), run comparison/diff, and the in-app notification center that later fronts the ITSM tier-2 work.

One suggestion beyond the roadmap: when the a11y theme gets picked up, it may be worth a short **ADR** (target level, exemptions, testing policy) — accessibility targets are exactly the kind of decision that benefits from a written record, since "WCAG 2.1 AA" quietly means different things to different auditors.

> DEVELOPER

And when we incorporate the data lineage, Maybe we can move to suite first to asset first. What do you think?

> AGENT

Yes — with one important refinement: don't *replace* suite-first with asset-first; **split the noun from the verb**. Assets become what users *browse and reason about* (health, lineage, incidents, blast radius), suites remain how checks *execute* (batching, scheduling, trigger bindings, notifications, sharing). Trying to make assets the primary object for everything would fight three structural facts: authz is suite-scoped (ADR 0027) and re-keying permissions to assets is a painful migration for little gain; scheduling/triggers/notifications are genuinely batch-level operational concepts ("run these together when the pipeline succeeds"); and GX itself is suite-shaped, so the engine grain stays suites regardless. The products that do this well (dbt with models-vs-jobs, Monte Carlo with assets-vs-monitors) all run exactly this two-axis model — asset-first navigation, execution groups underneath.

The deeper point you're circling, though, is right and worth making explicit: **lineage and the asset-first pivot need the same missing primitive — a first-class asset entity.** Today "the table" only exists implicitly inside `Suite.target` and check configs. Lineage needs asset nodes; the asset page needs asset identity; incidents need something to attach to; governance-catalog sync needs an entity to map to. That's one migration serving four features, and it should be built once, before any of them.

And there's a ready-made answer for the hardest part — asset *identity* (the same logical table reached via DEV vs QA connections, flat-file patterns as assets, UC three-level names): **adopt the OpenLineage dataset naming spec (namespace + name) as the canonical asset key from day one.** It's vendor-neutral, it makes the Theme-14 OpenLineage emission/pull interop automatic instead of a mapping layer, and it means DataQ's asset IDs are already speaking the same language as every catalog that might consume or feed them.

So the phased shape I'd record:

1. **Asset entity + resolution** (the schema work: `assets` keyed by OpenLineage naming, plus mapping checks/runs to asset IDs) — the enabler for everything below.
2. **Asset view** (already Theme 3) rides it as a read-only aggregation — with one authz subtlety: an asset page aggregates across suites, so it must filter to the caller's suite grants and not leak the existence of unshared checks (the same 404-no-leak discipline you verified live).
3. **Lineage lands** (Theme 14 pull/emit) → asset pages grow upstream/downstream + blast radius; the RCA dossier and G-d incidents attach to assets.
4. **Navigation inversion** — sidebar leads with Assets, dashboard health scores aggregate per asset (more meaningful to data consumers than per-suite), suites demote to an "execution groups" surface. Deep links and the suite CRUD keep working untouched.

Step 4 is the point where DataQ stops *feeling* like "GX-as-a-service" and starts feeling like a data-observability product — which is exactly the G-a/G-d repositioning the maturity assessment calls for. Want me to capture this as a design note in the roadmap — probably as an expansion of Theme 3's asset-view row plus a cross-ref from Theme 14's governance section and the G-d row, so the asset-entity-first sequencing isn't lost when the themes get picked up separately?
